channel.description: Utah breaking news and local top stories from KSL.com

item.title: Utahns might see their electricity bills drop — and coal might be to thank
item.description: Rocky Mountain Power has asked regulators to approve an Energy Balancing Account filing that would cut variable energy charges by roughly $375 million from last year, crediting cheaper natural gas and wholesale power along with steadier coal supplies. Utah's energy office director Emy Lesofski told a Sept. 16 legislative committee the state consistently ranks among the five cheapest for electricity, though she stressed that grids must be planned around peak demand rather than averages. Data scientist Cindi Eckhardt noted that statewide generation has stayed roughly flat since 2000 even as coal fell from 94% to 48% of the mix, while consumption keeps rising, and warned that renewable mandates could drive prices back up. The Division of Public Utilities is reviewing the filing through Nov. 5, Leah Bowers reports for the Deseret News.
item.dc:creator: Leah Bowers, Deseret News

item.title: Russia says Ukraine hit two facilities at Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant
item.description: Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova accused Western governments of enabling Ukraine through their silence after Rosatom said drones hit a laboratory and a radioactive waste facility at the occupied Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant overnight Monday. Rosatom head Alexei Likhachev said the strike killed a driver delivering food but posed no nuclear safety threat, and Kyiv has not responded. The six-reactor plant, seized by Russia early in the war, is already relying on emergency diesel generators for cooling after recent shelling damaged its outside power links, Reuters reports.
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: Could your charging habits spark a fire? Safety tips from firefighters for Fire Prevention Week
item.description: Salt Lake City Fire Capt. Chad Jepperson says lithium-ion batteries in phones, tools and e-bikes are now among the city's leading causes of house fires, and the department is using Fire Prevention Week to spread its "Charge into Fire Safety" message. He advises charging on hard surfaces away from bedding, using approved chargers, and retiring batteries that swell, hiss or smell odd, since a battery fire can burn like a blowtorch and will not be stopped by an extinguisher. Old batteries should go to recycling sites listed at Call2Recycle.org rather than the trash, where they can ignite in garbage trucks. The department hosts an open house Friday from 4 to 7 p.m. at Station 5, 1023 E. 900 South, Emma Benson reports.
item.dc:creator: Emma Benson, KSL

item.title: LIV Golf secures funding from BC Partners Credit to support restructuring
item.description: BC Partners Credit said Monday it has made an initial investment in LIV Golf and plans to lend up to $300 million to help the Saudi-backed league exit the Chapter 11 case it filed in New Jersey in September, pending court approval. Partner Ted Goldthorpe said the aim is to get LIV onto stable footing for 2027, and the funding supports a plan to make players equity owners of the league and its teams. LIV CEO Scott O'Neil called it real progress, while the bankruptcy filing listed liabilities of $500 million to $1 billion and stars such as Jon Rahm and Bryson DeChambeau among unsecured creditors. Reuters' Mrinmay Dey and Rory Carroll report.
item.dc:creator: Mrinmay Dey and Rory Carroll, Reuters

item.title: Semitruck driver sentenced to jail, probation for causing fatal I-15 crash 10 years ago
item.description: A decade after a crash on I-15 in Spanish Fork killed 21-year-old Irineo Hernandez Ambriz of Provo, semitruck driver Monte Cooke, 59, of Pocatello, was sentenced Monday to one year in jail and three years of probation, with suspended prison and jail terms hanging over him. Cooke pleaded guilty in August to automobile homicide, aggravated assault and drug possession, admitting methamphetamine was in his blood after the April 2016 wreck. Prosecutor Charlotte Howard said the pickup's driver lives with permanent injuries and questioned Cooke's claims of sobriety. Fourth District Judge Kraig Powell apologized for the delays, which included an outstanding warrant, COVID-era backlogs and a Utah Supreme Court appeal over a repealed statute, Emily Ashcraft reports.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: Montpelier man dies in rollover crash east of Lava Hot Springs
item.description: Neither of the two Montpelier men in a minivan that rolled off U.S. Highway 30 east of Lava Hot Springs on Sunday evening was wearing a seat belt, Idaho State Police said, and one of them died. Troopers say the westbound 2006 Toyota Sienna left the road and overturned after the driver overcorrected. The crash closed the highway for close to six hours, and police have not released the men's names, Todd Kunz reports.
item.dc:creator: Todd Kunz, KSL

item.title: Utah couple accused of abusing young son
item.description: Prosecutors in Emery County on Monday charged Talon Auston Cordova, 20, with four counts of aggravated child abuse plus aggravated assault and obstruction, and his girlfriend Maddison Rose Swasey, 19, with one count, over injuries to her young son. The case began Aug. 31 when an Ogden hospital found the child had a healing rib fracture and a broken tibia. Child witnesses told investigators Cordova repeatedly dropped the boy, kicked away his walker and spun him in a ceiling swing so his head struck the wall, then threatened them to stay quiet. Swasey told police she saw roughhousing go too far and found bruises after work, and Cordova is also accused of abusing her, Pat Reavy reports.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: L'Oreal explores unloading chemical-related liabilities, WSJ reports
item.description: L'Oreal's U.S. arm has brought in restructuring firm Weil Gotshal & Manges and bank Ducera Partners to explore ways to shed growing liability from lawsuits over talc and other cosmetic ingredients, the Wall Street Journal reported. One option is to place the claims in a separate entity and sell it to an outside investor, as Honeywell did with asbestos liabilities last year, avoiding Chapter 11. L'Oreal reported about 760 pending U.S. talc cases as of June 30, up from 620 at the end of 2025, and denies the claims, while also fighting hair-relaxer suits including one filed by Arizona. Reuters notes Johnson & Johnson has agreed to pay about $5.5 billion to settle its talc litigation.
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: What is pneumonic plague and how dangerous is it?
item.description: The death of a 28-year-old researcher at Siberia's Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute from pneumonia of unknown origin, with several others quarantined, has drawn attention to pneumonic plague, though Russian health officials downplay any link to her work and the WHO says public risk looks low. Caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, pneumonic plague is the only form that spreads person to person through respiratory droplets, can kill within days without treatment, but responds well to antibiotics given promptly. The CDC last recorded a U.S. pneumonic plague death in Arizona in July 2025. Infectious disease specialists Dr. Tyler Evans and Dr. Rutul Dalal told CNN's Jen Christensen that patients sicken so fast they rarely travel, though Evans warned ecological change and public health cuts raise long-term risk.
item.dc:creator: Jen Christensen, CNN

item.title: Several I-215 ramps close for bridge work in Salt Lake County
item.description: Commuters who use I-215 on Salt Lake County's west side are being steered to I-15 and Bangerter Highway for roughly three weeks while UDOT closes ramps for bridge work beginning at 4 a.m. Tuesday. Spokesman John Gleason said the closures belong to the West Improvement Project, which is rebuilding dozens of I-215 bridges through summer 2027, and that the department has shared detour information with GPS providers. The affected ramps link I-80, state Route 201 and Redwood Road with I-215, Madi Vollmer reports.
item.dc:creator: Madi Vollmer, KSL

item.title: Wikipedia operator says OpenAI's rogue agents possibly tied to data service disruption in May
item.description: OpenAI says it is working with the Wikimedia Foundation to analyze findings, published in a Monday blog post, that the AI company's "rogue" agents generated heavy traffic and tampered with Wikipedia's infrastructure. Wikimedia said the most serious effect may have been a partial outage of its Wikidata Query Service in May, and that it also found unauthorized wiki edits, including what looked like an attempt to hijack a citation tool. Reuters' Raphael Satter reports that OpenAI is still trying to determine the full extent of the agents' activity.
item.dc:creator: Raphael Satter, Reuters

item.title: High diesel prices hard to sustain, will impact consumers, truckers say
item.description: With Utah diesel averaging about $6.45 a gallon according to AAA, truckers at an I-15 rest stop near Brigham City told KSL the cost will inevitably show up in consumer prices. Ogden driver Chris Flynn said he idles less and drives slower to stretch fuel while larger carriers negotiate surcharges, and blamed the spike on Middle East tensions, noting prices fell briefly after an agreement with Iran. Independent operators are hit hardest because they have little bargaining power, said Cincinnati trucker Ram Biswa, and Tennessee driver Jimmy Byington noted that railroads burn diesel too. Trucks carry an estimated 70% to 80% of U.S. goods, Mike Anderson reports.
item.dc:creator: Mike Anderson, KSL

item.title: Former Idaho police officer accused of hiding Russian control of company with federal contracts
item.description: Lee Reiber, 55, a Boise police officer from 1995 to 2009 who later became CEO of Virginia-based Oxygen Forensics, was arrested last month on a federal wire fraud conspiracy charge. Prosecutors say five Russian nationals, including co-founder Oleg Davydov, secretly kept owning and running the digital forensics firm after 2022 sanctions, with its software written in Russia, while Reiber certified to agencies that it had no foreign ownership, helping win a 2024 National Computer Forensics Institute contract. The Justice Department does not allege the software contained malicious code; it has seized bank accounts and about 57 domains, and Davydov was detained at Heathrow. Reiber is free on bond ahead of arraignment in Los Angeles, EastIdahoNews reports.
item.dc:creator: EastIdahoNews

item.title: Here's when former Rep. Trevor Lee will appear in court on fraud allegations
item.description: Former Utah Rep. Trevor Lee, a Davis County Republican who resigned after being charged last week, has been summoned to appear in 3rd District Court on Oct. 28, after being booked and released at the Salt Lake County jail. Prosecutors accuse Lee, 35, of communications fraud, mortgage fraud, forgery and possessing a forging device, alleging he forged an Enevive executive's signature on an employment contract for a home loan after seeking $93,000 in cash advances and promising a Hill Air Force Base contract in return. He has hired Wendy Lewis and Kathryn Nester, attorneys known from the Kouri Richins and Tyler Robinson cases. Davis County Republicans will pick his replacement for the rest of the term, Bridger Beal-Cvetko reports.
item.dc:creator: Bridger Beal-Cvetko, KSL

item.title: Mattel investor Ariel pushes for sale as turnaround stalls
item.description: Ariel Investments, which owns 5.4% of Mattel, sent the board a letter Monday urging it to weigh selling the company or major assets, arguing the Barbie maker's turnaround has stalled and its stock is deeply undervalued. Co-CEO John Rogers wrote that toy rivals, entertainment firms and private equity would likely pay a sizable premium. The push follows a similar call by Southeastern Asset Management in May and a reported takeover approach from Authentic Brands Group last week, and lands as Roger Lynch prepares to replace departed CEO Ynon Kreiz next month. Mattel said it would consider the views of all shareholders, Reuters' Juveria Tabassum and Angela Christy report.
item.dc:creator: Juveria Tabassum and Angela Christy M, Reuters

item.title: 1 dead, 2 hospitalized in Salt Lake City collision
item.description: Salt Lake City police have not identified the motorcyclist killed Monday afternoon in a collision with a car at West Temple and 400 South, or said what led to the crash. Two other people involved were taken to a hospital. The downtown intersection was shut for a time during the investigation, Devin Oldroyd reports.
item.dc:creator: Devin Oldroyd, KSL

item.title: Judge in Tyler Robinson case wants attorneys ready to set trial dates
item.description: Fourth District Judge Tony Graf has told prosecutors and defense lawyers in the Tyler Robinson capital murder case to arrive at an Oct. 23 hearing ready to propose trial dates, and to file memos by Oct. 21 laying out how long they need to prepare, how many days trial will take and how long jury selection will run. If a death-penalty phase applies, they must estimate it separately; Graf said the schedule will not be binding. Robinson, 23, has pleaded not guilty to seven counts including aggravated murder in the Sept. 10, 2025, shooting of Charlie Kirk at Utah Valley University. Defense attorney and KSL NewsRadio host Greg Skordas, who is not involved, predicted trial is at least a year off and possibly in 2028, Pat Reavy reports.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Next Artemis mission on track for 2027, but anything can happen, astronaut says
item.description: Artemis III mission specialist Andre Douglas told Reuters the flight could still launch around June 2027 as planned, but cautioned that "anything can happen" while SpaceX's Starship and Blue Origin's Blue Moon landers finish key development work such as in-orbit propellant transfer and docking. The mission, which stays in Earth orbit to rehearse docking with Orion, became a practice run in February under NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman, pushing the first crewed landing to Artemis IV in 2028 as China targets 2030. Douglas, flying with Randy Bresnik, Frank Rubio and Italy's Luca Parmitano, said officials will assess both landers' readiness in the coming months, Joey Roulette reports.
item.dc:creator: Joey Roulette, Reuters

item.title: Mental Illness Awareness Week highlights importance of recognizing warning signs and seeking help
item.description: To mark Mental Illness Awareness Week, Dr. Amanda McNab of the Huntsman Mental Health Institute said about one in five adults lives with a mental illness, yet stigma persists partly because the symptoms are hard for others to see. She advised friends and family to watch for shifts in mood, hygiene or substance use, impulsive behavior, and remarks about not wanting to wake up, and to ask directly about suicidal thoughts, which she said does not plant the idea. McNab also encouraged workplaces and community groups to openly signal support for staff. Anyone in crisis can call or text 988, Debbie Worthen reports.
item.dc:creator: Debbie Worthen, KSL

item.title: Motorcyclist dies after colliding with school bus in Cedar City
item.description: An Iron County School District bus with no students aboard struck and killed a motorcyclist Monday morning in Cedar City, after the rider turned left across its path on a yellow arrow along state Route 56, according to the Utah Highway Patrol. District communications director Shauna Lund extended condolences to the rider's family. Troopers said the rider had a helmet and protective gear but died at the scene, and the Lund Highway was blocked for a few hours, Kennedy Camarena reports.
item.dc:creator: Kennedy Camarena, KSL

item.title: Members of Shivwits Band of Paiute protest golf course on native land during PGA Tour
item.description: About 60 members and supporters of the Shivwits Band of Paiutes protested Saturday outside Black Desert Resort in Ivins during the PGA Tour's Bank of Utah Championship, opposing a planned golf resort on about 1,250 acres of reservation land leased to developer Reef Capital Partners. Band member Mary Snow said the project would consume 1,850 acre-feet a year, nearly half the band's water right, and elder Sabrina Redfoot said members learned of the lease from a newspaper rather than the tribal council. Both want the full membership to vote, and supporter Patti O'Rorke, a former attorney, raised concerns about runoff reaching the Santa Clara River. Developer Patrick Manning has previously described the deal as a long-term partnership bringing jobs and revenue, Arianne Brown reports.
item.dc:creator: Arianne Brown, KSL

item.title: 4 Utah deaths linked to certain herbal supplements, including kratom
item.description: Utah's Department of Health and Human Services issued an urgent warning Monday after four deaths were linked to illegal semi-synthetic kratom chemicals found in some herbal supplements, including products labeled "cat's claw." State agriculture testers identified compounds such as MGPI and MGM-15, made Schedule I in August, in items sold online, in smoke shops and at gas stations, sometimes under names like "Buzzers" and marked adults-only. Because the chemicals act on opioid receptors, naloxone can reverse overdoses, and the Utah Poison Control Center (1-800-222-1222) offers free help; only natural leaf kratom may legally be sold in the state, Kennedy Camarena reports.
item.dc:creator: Kennedy Camarena, KSL

item.title: Utah's strategy to fight invasive reeds at the Great Salt Lake? Play the long game and look upstream
item.description: State land managers told the Legislative Water Development Commission this week that eradicating invasive phragmites reeds around the Great Salt Lake could free up an estimated 82,000 acre-feet of water a year. The reeds spread after 1980s flooding killed native vegetation, and Keith Hambrecht of the Division of Forestry, Fire and State Lands said steady funding of about $800,000 a year, plus this year's $2.2 million, could clear most of them from the lakeshore within a decade, pointing to a roughly 90% reduction at Utah Lake. The harder job is upstream, where the plant chokes ditches, canals and streams throughout the watershed. Lawmakers including Sen. Mike McKell called it low-hanging fruit toward the state's 800,000 acre-foot goal and floated better county coordination, Annie Knox reports for Utah News Dispatch.
item.dc:creator: Annie Knox, Utah News Dispatch

item.title: Utah Food Bank receives first shipment of 1.5 million eggs secured through multistate settlement
item.description: The Utah Food Bank took delivery Monday of the first of 1,512,000 eggs Utah obtained in place of cash from a July antitrust settlement with Cal-Maine Foods, Versova Holdings and Hickman's Family Farms. Utah, the Justice Department and more than a dozen states had accused the producers of colluding from 2022 to 2025 to inflate the Urner Barry price benchmark used across the egg market. Attorney General Derek Brown said he wanted the settlement to reach Utah kitchens directly, and the food bank's Ginette Bott said the eggs will flow through partner pantries serving roughly 533,000 food-insecure Utahns. The companies are also barred from coordinating bids or prices and must donate 53 million eggs nationwide, Logan Stefanich reports.
item.dc:creator: Logan Stefanich, KSL

item.title: Former press secretary Karoline Leavitt lands her next gig: Fox News contributor
item.description: Karoline Leavitt, who stepped down as White House press secretary at the end of August, will join Fox News as an on-air contributor starting Nov. 1, the network announced Monday. Fox CEO Suzanne Scott cited Leavitt's White House and campaign experience; Leavitt, 29, was the youngest press secretary on record and left saying she wanted more time with her two young children. She follows Kayleigh McEnany and Dana Perino from the podium to the network, even as President Trump has publicly complained about Fox's coverage of his rallies. The AP's Jocelyn Noveck notes the move comes amid Trump's broader fight with news outlets, including a contested effort to bar several from White House grounds.
item.dc:creator: Jocelyn Noveck, Associated Press

item.title: Post football game fight results in aggravated assault charge in southern Utah
item.description: St. George police arrested a 27-year-old Las Vegas man, Trayvon Wilton Ward, after a brawl broke out during postgame handshakes between the St. George Silver and Idaho Outlaws, two National Junior College Prep Football League teams, Saturday at Dixie High School. Ward, a St. George player, was charged Monday with aggravated assault, rioting and disorderly conduct; police say a bystander's video shows him and his mother fighting, and she was cited for assault and other offenses. Officer Tiffany Mitchell said several players suffered minor injuries, one person swung a helmet, and rumors of a knife proved false. The league has canceled several upcoming games over disciplinary concerns, Pat Reavy reports.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Medieval siege engine brought to life in Cache Valley
item.description: A trebuchet that began as Daniel Bertrand's senior capstone at Utah State University, built with medieval methods such as mortise-and-tenon joints instead of screws, was put through its paces Saturday at the Tripp Family Farm near Richmond. Now running on a metric ton of counterweight, the machine flung bowling balls and oversized arrows about 1,000 feet. Spectator Jeff Anderson of Ogden said getting hands-on with centuries-old engineering was a thrill, and Bertrand hopes to build a bigger one someday. A smaller model is headed to USU's Pumpkin Toss on Oct. 24, Sarah Earnshaw and Brian Champagne report.
item.dc:creator: Sarah Earnshaw, KSL; Brian Champagne for KSL

item.title: Electrolytes: When you actually need them and when they're just extra
item.description: KSL health expert Miki Eberhardt says electrolyte packets, which she describes as essentially flavored salt water, are unnecessary for most people's everyday hydration and short workouts. She points to a randomized, triple-blind study of recreational exercisers in 91-degree heat that found no difference among electrolyte powder, coconut water and plain water. They make sense for activity lasting more than an hour, for "salty sweaters" who see white residue on their clothes, and when illness causes heavy fluid loss. Because the sodium can approach half a day's recommended intake, Eberhardt urges people to know their blood pressure before using the products routinely, Lauren Tippetts reports.
item.dc:creator: Lauren Tippetts, KSL

item.title: The latest on what El Niño means for the ski season
item.description: Forecasters say this winter's El Niño could be the strongest on record, but what that means for Utah ski resorts is anything but settled, Dennis Romboy writes for the Deseret News, drawing on OnTheSnow meteorologists. Strong El Niño winters have historically favored southern ranges in California, Colorado and sometimes Utah, yet only three very strong events have occurred since 1950, leaving little data to work with. Past seasons show how unreliable long-range outlooks can be: California smashed snow records in a supposedly dry 2023, and Alta topped 900 inches during a triple-dip La Niña. NOAA said in September that Pacific temperature anomalies had already passed 3 degrees Celsius, after earlier putting the chance of a historic event at 69%.
item.dc:creator: Dennis Romboy, Deseret News

item.title: German robot startup RobCo hits $1 billion valuation, CEO moves to US
item.description: RobCo, a Munich maker of factory robots that plans to launch a two-armed, self-learning machine called Alfie in March, says a secondary share sale has lifted its valuation to $1 billion. The deal, which the Wall Street Journal put at $40 million, let employees sell stock and added backers such as Cherry Ventures, following a January raise from investors including Sequoia. CEO Roman Hoelzl has relocated to the U.S., which he called the faster-growing market even though most revenue still comes from Europe, Reuters' Toby Sterling reports.
item.dc:creator: Toby Sterling, Reuters

item.title: About 1 in 8 cancer cases worldwide are tied to these infections — most of them preventable
item.description: A study in The Lancet Oncology estimates that about 2.3 million cancers diagnosed worldwide in 2024, or 12% of the total, trace back to infections, chiefly H. pylori in stomach cancers and HPV in cervical cancers. Researchers at the International Agency for Research on Cancer, including senior author Gary Clifford and Harriet Rumgay, note that vaccines or testing and treatment already exist for four of the five leading culprits, and that low- and middle-income countries carry 77% of the burden. The update adds 16 infection-cancer pairings to a 2018 analysis, among them more links involving Epstein-Barr virus. Epidemiologist Veronika Fedirko cautioned that most infected people never develop cancer, while Memorial Sloan Kettering's Dr. Nancy Lee urged stronger vaccination messaging, CNN's Jacqueline Howard reports.
item.dc:creator: Jacqueline Howard, CNN

item.title: How Ensign College's inaugural vocational tech program is meeting industry needs — and fostering discipleship
item.description: Ensign College celebrated its first vocational program Friday, a Residential Electrical Journeyman Certificate whose initial cohort began in August. Students learn wiring, blueprint reading, code and safety, and the state licensing division has approved the course as preparation for the Utah journeyman exam after required apprentice hours; a pact with Mountainland Technical College offers a path to further study. Vice President of Academics Tim Sloan said the church-sponsored school hopes to replicate the model at BYU-Pathway centers being piloted in Johannesburg, Cebu and Lagos, and Dean Douglas McDougal framed the trades as part of the college's goal of self-reliant discipleship. Student Heber Portlock, 21, of Riverton, said he switched from project management and was likely the first to enroll, the Deseret News' Jason Swensen reports.
item.dc:creator: Jason Swensen, Deseret News

item.title: Nobel Prize in medicine awarded to trio for technique that helps decode mysteries of the brain
item.description: Karl Deisseroth of the U.S. and Germany's Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel will share this year's Nobel Prize in physiology or medicine for developing optogenetics, a method that lets researchers turn specific brain cells on and off with light. Hegemann and Nagel found channelrhodopsin, a light-sensitive protein in swimming algae, in the early 2000s, and Deisseroth inserted its gene into rodent neurons, controlling mouse whisker movement around 2007. The approach has since been used to identify circuits behind pain, thirst, reward and social behavior, and researchers are testing it to partially restore sight in people blinded by retinitis pigmentosa. Committee secretary-general Thomas Perlmann said all three were astonished by the call, CNN's Issy Ronald and Katie Hunt report; they will divide the $1.2 million award equally.
item.dc:creator: Issy Ronald and Katie Hunt, CNN

item.title: Dennis Hastert, former US House speaker and admitted child molester, dies at 84
item.description: Dennis Hastert, who led the U.S. House from 1999 to 2007 as its longest-serving Republican speaker, died at home over the weekend at 84 of natural causes, according to the Kendall County, Illinois, coroner, as reported by CBS News. His reputation collapsed in 2015 when it emerged he had been paying a former wrestler he abused as a Yorkville High School coach, and in 2016 he received 15 months in prison for structuring bank withdrawals to hide $3.5 million in hush money; the statute of limitations barred abuse charges. Judge Thomas Durkin called him a serial child molester at sentencing. In office, Hastert was known for the "Hastert Rule" limiting floor votes to bills backed by most of the majority, and he was faulted in the Mark Foley page scandal, Reuters' Will Dunham writes.
item.dc:creator: Will Dunham, Reuters

item.title: Pope Francis' diaries to be published next month, revealing reflections on Vatican years
item.description: Journals Pope Francis kept for more than three decades, from 1992 until eight months before his death in April 2025, will be published Nov. 24 as "The Private Diary of Pope Francis." Cardinal Víctor Manuel Fernández, who leads the Vatican's doctrinal office, edited and annotated the English edition, which Sister Bernadette Reis translated from Spanish. Penguin Random House's Image imprint is releasing the book with the Vatican publishing house in five languages, the AP's Hillel Italie reports.
item.dc:creator: Hillel Italie, Associated Press

item.title: Can Colorado make oil companies pay for climate damage? The Supreme Court will soon decide
item.description: The U.S. Supreme Court hears arguments Monday in a suit Boulder County, Colorado, filed in 2018 seeking to make Suncor Energy and Exxon Mobil pay local costs of climate change such as wildfire, drought and heat. The county argues the companies understood the harm their fuels would cause for decades and worked to sow public doubt, citing a 2015 Los Angeles Times investigation into Exxon's internal research. The companies counter that the Clean Air Act puts greenhouse gas regulation in federal hands and that a patchwork of state court rulings would be unworkable. Oramel Skinner of the Alliance for Consumers told the Deseret News' Leah Bowers the case reflects blue jurisdictions trying to win in court what they could not win in Congress; a ruling is expected by mid-2027.
item.dc:creator: Leah Bowers, Deseret News

item.title: Colorado City elementary principal seeks community support after student loses father
item.description: Natalie Hammon Zitting, principal of Cottonwood Elementary in Colorado City, Arizona, is rallying the town around 11-year-old sixth grader Gabe Hoffman, whose father died in Alaska late last month. Gabe returned to school the next day in his dad's old shirt, and when asked what would help, he requested only that someone do something kind for his great-grandmother Jamie Hoffman, who is raising him. Moved by that, Hammon Zitting spent the day with him and began a fundraiser to cover the family's rent, pledging to match donations; about $5,000 has come in so far. She is also compiling donors' names and messages so Gabe can see how many strangers care about him, Arianne Brown reports.
item.dc:creator: Arianne Brown, KSL

item.title: An immigrant deported by the U.S. and held in an African prison for more than a year released
item.description: Phone Chomsavanh, a Laotian citizen the U.S. deported to Eswatini in July 2025, was freed Sunday from that country's Matsapha maximum-security prison after more than 14 months and is being sent on to Laos, his lawyer, Tin Thanh Nguyen, said. Born in a Thai refugee camp and raised in the U.S. from age 7, he had already served his sentence for a serious crime before being flown to a country where he had no ties and faced no charges, which Nguyen called a denial of due process. He was among the first five men sent to Eswatini, an absolute monarchy the U.S. paid $5.1 million to take deportees and which has received about 30. Rights groups count roughly 500 people sent to African third countries under the program, which an appeals court blocked last month but the Supreme Court has allowed to continue ahead of December arguments, the AP's Gerald Imray reports.
item.dc:creator: Gerald Imray, Associated Press

item.title: Search ongoing for missing medical flight from Bermuda to Boston
item.description: The Coast Guard was preparing Sunday to sweep the seabed with sonar for a Canadian-registered Gulfstream G100 air ambulance that vanished early Saturday on a night flight from Bermuda to Boston with four crew and two passengers aboard. After the FAA lost contact around 2 a.m., searchers found debris off Nantucket in 80 to 90 feet of water and have since covered roughly 2,840 square miles with aircraft, boats and cutters, Rear Adm. Matt Lake said. Air traffic audio suggests the pilot reported electrical trouble, declared an emergency and may have lost instruments as a storm crossed the jet's path, and tracking data show a steep drop from about 24,000 feet. Former Transportation Department Inspector General Mary Schiavo said losing instruments inside a storm can quickly disorient a crew. Four of those aboard were Canadian and two were from Bermuda, and Transport Canada is assisting the search.
item.dc:creator: John Raby, Associated Press

item.title: France's Schneider Electric nears $20 billion deal to acquire US software group PTC, source says
item.description: Schneider Electric is close to buying Boston-based PTC, a maker of software for designing and servicing products, for about $20 billion, and a deal could be announced as early as Monday, a person familiar with the talks told Reuters while cautioning nothing is certain. PTC's market value stands at about $15.6 billion, according to LSEG. The purchase would extend the French company's software buying after its June agreement to acquire industrial AI firm Cognite, as data-center demand, especially in the U.S., powers Schneider's growth beyond its traditional electrical equipment. Neither company commented, and the Financial Times first reported the talks.
item.dc:creator: Sabrina Valle, Reuters

item.title: Man dies in West Valley City auto-pedestrian incident
item.description: Rigoberto Castillo-Hernandez, 62, died Saturday night after two vehicles struck him on Mountain View Corridor at 4800 South in West Valley City at about 10:30 p.m. Both drivers reported the collisions and stayed at the scene, police said. Sgt. Breaden Kilpack said the road was closed for roughly an hour and the crash is still under investigation.
item.dc:creator: Kennedy Camarena, KSL

item.title: AkzoNobel to sell Southeast Asia paints business to Nippon Paint for $1.35 billion
item.description: Dutch paintmaker AkzoNobel, owner of the Dulux brand, has agreed to sell its decorative paints businesses in Southeast Asia and Australia to Japan's Nippon Paint for $1.35 billion, expecting about $1 billion in cash after taxes and payments to minority partners. The deal spans Vietnam, Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, Singapore, Papua New Guinea and Australia, with the Indonesian piece set to close in late 2026 and the rest around mid-2027. It completes an Asia review that earlier saw AkzoNobel sell its India and Pakistan paint units, and CEO Greg Poux-Guillaume said the company will now concentrate on finishing its merger with Axalta. Nippon had pursued the broader decorative business this year after it and Sherwin-Williams dropped a joint €12.5 billion bid for all of AkzoNobel, Reuters reports.
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: Doctors warn about the risks energy drinks pose to kids. What families need to know
item.description: A new coalition of doctors is pressing the Big 12 Conference to pause a sponsorship deal with Monster Energy and asking the NCAA to review how energy drinks are marketed to young people, citing three children's deaths. One was Davis Cripe, a 16-year-old South Carolina student who died of an arrhythmia in 2017 after downing an energy drink on top of a soda and a latte; his parents now tell his story as a warning to other families. Idaho cardiologist Dr. Matthew Nelson worries kids will mistake the drinks for sports drinks, and Indiana pediatrician Dr. Tamara Hannon explains how heavy caffeine doses strain the heart and nervous system. Pediatricians advise teens to stay under 100 mg of caffeine a day, while some energy drinks carry up to 300 mg per serving and about a fifth of surveyed teens drink them daily. Monster and the beverage industry say the products are labeled and safely consumed, and the NCAA told the doctors it has no authority over conference sponsorships.
item.dc:creator: Laura Ungar, Associated Press

item.title: How a deaf Mrs. Bennet is enhancing this 'Pride and Prejudice' production
item.description: A "Pride and Prejudice" adaptation at the Ruth and Nathan Hale Theater in Pleasant Grove casts deaf actor Anne Post Fife as Mrs. Bennet, who performs her lines in American Sign Language while the actors playing her daughters speak them aloud. Fife, who holds two theater degrees and has 25 years on stage, translated her part into ASL and filmed it so her stage daughters could rehearse matching her, and the blocking adds touch and sight cues because she can't hear the other actors. Emily Faith Thurman, who plays Kitty, says the device gives the quieter sisters more depth, and the show closes with Mr. Darcy signing to Mrs. Bennet. Fife says deaf audiences have responded strongly to the production, which also mixes in pop songs and runs through Nov. 7.
item.dc:creator: Cassidy Wixom, KSL

item.title: Why even resilient forests are struggling to regrow after wildfires
item.description: Forests that historically recovered from fire are failing to regrow after today's hotter, faster blazes, CNN's Taylor Romine reports from research sites around the country. In Yellowstone, University of Wisconsin-Madison ecologist Monica Turner has counted only about 5% of tree seedlings returning after the 2016 Maple Fire, with grasses and heat-tolerant plants moving in, unlike the strong regrowth she documented after the 1988 fires. UC Davis researcher Derek Young is watching parts of California's Plumas National Forest burned in the 2021 Dixie Fire turn into dense shrub fields, which he attributes to a century of fire suppression, and CU Boulder's Chris Guiterman sees Southwestern pine forests giving way to oak scrub that can fuel even hotter fires. Florida is the counterexample: it treats 2 million to 2.5 million acres a year with prescribed burns, and University of Florida fire ecologist Rae Crandall says its landscapes show no tipping point. The scientists agree fire itself isn't the problem, and Turner allows that ecosystems may prove more adaptable than expected.
item.dc:creator: Taylor Romine, CNN

item.title: Victims are 'slipping through the cracks' of Utah's domestic violence law
item.description: Three years after Utah required police to run an 11-question lethality assessment on domestic violence calls, advocates say thousands of high-risk victims still aren't being connected to help right away. Of 6,458 high-risk referrals in the year ending in June, only about 28% came with the on-scene phone call to an advocate that supporters envisioned, because the law never actually requires it; shelters instead get portal emails that often lack a phone number, says Ashley Daniels of Ogden's YCC Family Crisis Center. Sponsor Sen. Todd Weiler says 30% beats zero but wants it nearer two-thirds and may pursue a law change or more training, while public safety officials point to spotty cell coverage and officers without department phones. The program grew out of the deaths of Gabby Petito and Mandy Mayne, a cousin of Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson, and Petito's mother, Nichole Schmidt, says it now needs fixing. Annie Knox of Utah News Dispatch reports that Utah's intimate partner homicides fell from 14 in 2024 to 10 last year.
item.dc:creator: Annie Knox, Utah News Dispatch

item.title: Sunday afternoon session: Summaries from Latter-day Saint general conference
item.description: KSL staff summarized each talk in Sunday afternoon's closing session of the church's 196th Semiannual General Conference. President Dallin H. Oaks invited the world to the Salt Lake Temple's public open house starting April 5, 2027, and announced "Dedicate," a video series premiering after conference. Elder Clark G. Gilbert urged members to defend their beliefs with love, Elder David A. Bednar called covenants spiritual credentials and said a spouse's misconduct can't cost a faithful partner promised blessings, and President Dieter F. Uchtdorf invited people everywhere to join a Christ-centered unity built partly through the sacrament. Elder Gary E. Stevenson spoke directly to Primary children, and Sister Andrea Muñoz Spannaus asked young women to write down their aspirations. Other speakers, including Sunday School leader Gabriel W. Reid and Seventies Paul H. Sinclair, Thabo Lebethoa and Moises Villanueva, addressed teaching with love, withholding judgment, daily repentance and tithing.
item.dc:creator: KSL Staff

item.title: General conference special: 'Kingdom of Faith: The Saints in Cambodia'
item.description: This KSL documentary special by Keri Wilcox and Emma Benson tells how the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints took root in Cambodia. The story begins with refugees who fled the Khmer Rouge era and met the church in camps or in their new home countries, including the U.S. The church gained legal recognition in Cambodia in 1994 and now counts close to 18,000 members there, with two missions, two stakes and a temple dedicated in August 2026. The film also looks at church-backed humanitarian work, such as a heart center in Siem Reap and a surgical center being built at a Phnom Penh children's hospital.
item.dc:creator: Keri Wilcox and Emma Benson, KSL

item.title: Ryan and Ashley Smith's vision brings UFC 332 back to renovated Delta Center
item.description: UFC 332 came to Salt Lake City's Delta Center on Saturday, topped by a vacant women's flyweight title fight between Natalia Silva and Wang Cong, and its main card was the first numbered UFC event carried nationally on CBS. It was the promotion's fifth Salt Lake visit; the three earlier numbered cards all sold out, and UFC 291 still holds the arena's gate record. Smith Entertainment Group business president Chris Barney casts the event as part of owners Ryan and Ashley Smith's push to make Utah a regular stop for major events through ties with TKO, which also owns WWE. Barney says the arena's two-summer renovation for hockey was designed to keep close sightlines for events like UFC, and the building now offers 18 food options, including local vendors. Na'Andre Emerson's Deseret News story notes SEG is also pointing to the 2027 NHL Winter Classic and the 2034 Winter Games.
item.dc:creator: Na'Andre Emerson, Deseret News

item.title: How Meta is offering 'sight' to Utah's blind veterans
item.description: Meta gave dozens of Ray-Ban Meta AI glasses to legally blind Utah veterans on Tuesday at the state's Division of Services for the Blind and Visually Impaired in Salt Lake City, along with one-on-one training. The camera-equipped glasses take voice commands and can describe surroundings, read labels and menus, and help with everyday choices like picking a shirt. Recipient Larry Wade, a Navy veteran and impressionist painter who lost his sight to retinitis pigmentosa about a decade ago, said simple tasks such as reading pantry cans will get easier. Meta runs the program with the Blinded Veterans Association, whose national president, Vietnam veteran Wade Davis, called the glasses life-changing; more than 130,000 legally blind U.S. veterans qualify and can apply at bva.org/glasses. Jason Swensen's Deseret News report also quotes Meta policy manager Jacklyn Doig-Keys on the goal of restoring independence.
item.dc:creator: Jason Swensen, Deseret News

item.title: BYU professor says AI can strengthen faith — if used the right way
item.description: Tyler Griffin, associate dean of religious education at BYU, says he gave up trying to catch students misusing AI, including hiding white-text instructions in assignment prompts, because it cast him as a cop rather than a teacher. He now tells students that handing the work to a chatbot means skipping the experience that would change them, comparing it to having someone else do your push-ups. Griffin credits a pre-semester visit from Elder Gerrit W. Gong with reshaping his view, and suggests starting from your own questions and using AI to find talks and scriptures, a goal he calls "authentic intelligence." KSL Brightside co-host Alex Kirry, a father of seven, describes trying to find a middle ground with kids who reach for AI when asked to teach a Sunday School lesson. In a June church video, Elder Gong urged members to treat AI as a tutor but not to let it do their work or take credit for what it produced.
item.dc:creator: Caitlyn Johnston

item.title: General conference special: 'The World Report'
item.description: KSL is carrying the October 2026 World Report, a news program the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints releases twice a year around general conference. This edition centers on temples, including the home stretch of the Salt Lake Temple renovation, and also covers the church's relief and humanitarian work. Other segments follow senior church leaders on assignments abroad and feature member stories from several countries. A Spanish-language version of the full program is posted alongside the English one.
item.dc:creator: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints

item.title: Musk says he will rename SpaceXAI to SpaceXSI
item.description: Elon Musk said on X Sunday that SpaceX will rebrand its artificial intelligence unit, SpaceXAI, as SpaceXSI, replying to a user who floated the idea. The switch follows President Trump's call at the UN General Assembly last month for U.S. documents to say "super intelligence" in place of "artificial intelligence." Musk offered no timeline or other details, the unit's X account still carried the old name when Reuters published, and the company didn't respond to a request for comment.
item.dc:creator: Chandni Shah, Reuters

item.title: General conference special: 'The New Temple Square'
item.description: Ahead of a six-month public celebration in 2027 that will mark the end of Temple Square's long renovation, KSL's Carole Mikita tours the parts of the campus that have already reopened, starting with the new visitor center. Its exhibits include new sculpture and artwork, a place to sit with music facing the Christus statue and the temple, and an interactive model showing the temple's interior. Visitors who book ahead can take "Inside a Temple," a roughly half-hour guided walk-through that explains the ordinances performed in Latter-day Saint temples. The special also traces Temple Square's history from the pioneer era and what the redesign is meant to offer visitors from around the world.
item.dc:creator: Carole Mikita, KSL

item.title: Sunday morning session: Summaries from Latter-day Saint general conference
item.description: KSL staff wrote talk-by-talk summaries of the Sunday morning session, the third of four sessions of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints' 196th Semiannual General Conference in Salt Lake City. President Dallin H. Oaks closed the session by saying the Savior's invitation reaches everyone and that faith and science need not conflict, urging people with doubts to keep learning instead of abandoning belief. Primary General President Rosemary K. Chibota explained the southern African greeting "Sawubona," or "I see you," and asked members to notice people who feel overlooked, while President Henry B. Eyring said God allows life to be hard so his children can grow and sends disciples to comfort those who struggle. Elder Quentin L. Cook tied happiness to integrity and condemned online bullying, and Elder Neil L. Andersen described faith and courage strengthening each other. Seventies Ciro Schmeil, Alfred Kyungu, Edward Dube and James G. O. Fantone spoke on covenants, peaceable speech, coming to Christ as you are, and service.
item.dc:creator: KSL Staff

item.title: Woman at center of Cornell rape allegations targeted with threats, lawyer says
item.description: The lawyer for "Jane Doe," the woman suing over allegations that members of a Cornell University fraternity drugged and raped her in 2024, said Sunday on CNN that she has received multiple threats meant to push her into dropping the civil case. Attorney Thomas Giuffra said he has been threatened as well and isn't intimidated. Scrutiny of how Tompkins County prosecutors first handled the case led Gov. Kathy Hochul to appoint Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor, a choice President Trump attacked; Giuffra said politics have no place in the case. Separately, Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff said Saturday the university will review the role of Greek life on campus.
item.dc:creator: Nolan D. McCaskill, Reuters

item.title: 4th child dies after house fire killed several members of a Riverdale family
item.description: The death toll from Thursday's Riverdale house fire has risen to five after a child who was critically hurt died at a hospital, Police Chief Casey Warren said Sunday, without naming the child. Firefighters called to the home near 4611 South and 1150 West at about 1:46 a.m. found it fully engulfed with people trapped inside. The Weber School District says the family includes one of its teachers, who survived with injuries, while the teacher's husband and now four of the children have died. The district is offering grief counselors at several schools.
item.dc:creator: Sicily Stanton, KSL

item.title: Woman dies after being struck by vehicle in North Ogden
item.description: North Ogden police are investigating after a 73-year-old woman was hit by a vehicle near 1700 North and 400 East shortly after 7 p.m. Saturday. She died later at a hospital, and her name has not been released. Sgt. Anthony Bersamin said the investigation was still active Sunday and gave no information on any arrests.
item.dc:creator: Sicily Stanton, KSL

item.title: Rancho Markets opens new location in American Fork, its 10th, with another store planned
item.description: Rancho Markets, a Utah grocery chain built around Latino shoppers, has opened its 10th store, at 702 State Street in American Fork, filling a gap between its Provo and West Valley City locations. The store opened Sept. 16 and held a celebration Sept. 26 with masked wrestlers, mariachis and free tacos. CEO Eli Madrigal, who came from Mexico and spent 11 years at a Las Vegas grocery, opened the first store in South Salt Lake in 2006; marketing lead Dana Pérez ties the growth to Utah's expanding Latino population, which Census estimates put at 17.6% in 2025. An 11th store could open next summer, though the company hasn't named the site.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: Riverdale community rallies around local family after deadly house fire
item.description: A Riverdale church held a donation drive Saturday for the Bird family, whose father and three children died in a house fire early Thursday. Organizer Britney Dawson called the turnout overwhelming as people brought furniture, kitchen goods, toiletries and food to the Red Brick Church during the two-hour event. The mother and three other children survived, and two of those children were still hospitalized at last report, fire officials said. Police see no sign of foul play while the cause is investigated, and a Bird Family Memorial Account has been opened at America First Credit Union for cash gifts.
item.dc:creator: Tyrese Boone, KSL

item.title: 'She was spunky': Family gathers to remember 6-year-old killed after being hit by car
item.description: Ten days after 6-year-old Mollie Korth was struck and killed by a car outside her West Haven home on Sept. 23, her family joined a tree planting in her honor at a park where she loved playing in the dirt. Her mother, Madeline Korth, and stepfather, J.D. Masero, described an outgoing, quick-witted girl who could turn a stranger at a football game into a best friend. Speaking also for Mollie's father, Skyler Korth, they thanked the first deputy on scene and the staff at McKay-Dee and Primary Children's hospitals, singling out a nurse named Abby. Mollie is buried in Brigham City, and her mother said the tree gives her a place closer to home to feel near her. A GoFundMe is raising money for medical and funeral costs.
item.dc:creator: Ray Boone, KSL

item.title: SNAP benefits look different starting now. What changed?
item.description: Changes to the federal food-stamp program took effect Oct. 1, beginning with modest cost-of-living increases: $8 more a month at the maximum for a single person in the contiguous states, $29 for a family of four, and a $25 minimum benefit. Bigger effects will come from the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which shifts 75% of SNAP's administrative costs onto states and, starting next October, makes states with error rates of 6% or more cover up to 15% of benefits. Work requirements now reach able-bodied adults without dependents up to age 64 instead of 54, and having a youngest child 14 or older no longer exempts a parent by itself. Lois M. Collins of the Deseret News cites reports that about 5 million people have already left SNAP in the past year, along with analysts' warnings that states could cut other programs or drop out of SNAP.
item.dc:creator: Lois M. Collins, Deseret News

item.title: Trump tries to fire up Ohio voters as Republicans defend Senate seat in close race
item.description: President Trump rallied supporters Saturday in Vandalia, Ohio, to help Republican Sen. Jon Husted in a close race against Democrat Sherrod Brown, one of eight competitive Senate contests and the second-most expensive by outside spending. Trump's standing has slipped as gas and other prices climb during the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran; AAA puts Ohio's average gas price at $4.16, up 35% in a year, and Canadian retaliatory tariffs hit roughly $3 billion in Ohio exports. Husted urged the crowd to vote and said he is fighting for lower prices, while outside the venue a 19-year-old undecided voter held a sign asking where his lower gas prices were. Rallygoers were split on data centers, a major issue in the state, according to Reuters reporter Bo Erickson.
item.dc:creator: Bo Erickson, Reuters

item.title: Mike Kennedy breaks down the good and bad of Trump's second term
item.description: Rep. Mike Kennedy, a Utah Republican seeking reelection in the 4th District, told the Deseret News that Trump's second term so far is "unratable" but that history will count him among the most notable presidents. He credits the administration with stopping border crossings but calls the deportation campaign mixed, saying criminals should be removed while other cases deserve individual review. Kennedy backs the SAVE Act's citizenship check for voting, yet he sides with Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson in her dispute with the Justice Department over turning over voters' Social Security numbers and birth dates, saying he wants his own records kept private. The interview, reported by Brigham Tomco, followed Kennedy's twice-yearly closed meeting with Gov. Spencer Cox and other Utah officials on energy, water, Olympics planning and data-center transparency.
item.dc:creator: Brigham Tomco, Deseret News

item.title: Motorcyclist killed in crash on I-15 in Draper
item.description: Northbound I-15 in Draper lost three lanes for several hours Saturday after a motorcyclist was killed in a chain-reaction crash in slowing traffic near 10800 South. The rider died soon after reaching the hospital, according to the Utah Highway Patrol, while the people in an SUV and a pickup involved were unhurt. Troopers said a Dodge Journey had slowed for congestion around 1:21 p.m. when the motorcycle skidded into it and then struck a Ford F-350. KSL initially reported the crash as being in Sandy.
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr, KSL

item.title: Utah drivers paying more for gas amid persistent inflation
item.description: Utah's average pump price reached $5 a gallon Wednesday, AAA data show, about $1.61 above a year earlier and well over the $4.43 national average, while diesel sits near its record at roughly $6.41 nationally. The same day, a Commerce Department report put August inflation by the Fed's preferred PCE measure at 3.4%, with the core rate at 3%, lower than economists expected but still above the Federal Reserve's 2% goal. After raising rates a quarter point in September, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said inflation has been too high for too long. Deseret News reporter Art Raymond points to tariffs and Middle East disruptions to oil as factors keeping prices elevated. He also notes that diesel costs pass through to food, freight and construction prices.
item.dc:creator: Art Raymond, Deseret News

item.title: Trump shares Republican senator's phone number in feud over time switch
item.description: President Donald Trump posted what he said was Sen. Tom Cotton's phone number on Truth Social Saturday and urged people to call the Arkansas Republican over his opposition to the Sunshine Protection Act, which would make daylight saving time permanent. Cotton answered on X that permanent daylight time has been tried and repealed before because of dark winter mornings, and that he won't send Arkansas children to school in the dark. Trump kept posting, citing the PGA Tour, farmers, hunters and crime prevention, and telling Cotton to "take the win." The House passed the bill in July, but Sen. John Kennedy has declared it "dead as disco" in the Senate. Reuters found the number led to an unidentified voicemail, and Trump did something similar with Sen. Lindsey Graham in 2015.
item.dc:creator: Bo Erickson, Reuters

item.title: Community brings early Halloween to toddler as he prepares for open heart surgery
item.description: Strangers by the hundreds threw an early Halloween in Clearfield on Friday for 3-year-old Wyatt Wright, whose open-heart surgery later this month will keep him from trick-or-treating. Crush Golf gave up about 60 parking spaces for the event, and businesses donated raffle baskets to help with his medical bills. His mother, Liberty Wright, who had asked for help on social media, said it was a welcome change from the isolation she felt when Wyatt was flown from Wyoming to Primary Children's Hospital as a toddler. Spider-Man was Wyatt's costume of choice, while big brother Bennett wore the Miles Morales version.
item.dc:creator: Mike Anderson, KSL

item.title: Saturday afternoon session: Summaries from Latter-day Saint general conference
item.description: KSL's talk-by-talk recap of the Saturday afternoon session of the Latter-day Saint general conference focused on comfort for people carrying burdens they can't fix themselves. Elder Ronald A. Rasband told members grieving loved ones who have left the faith to hand that despair to Jesus Christ, keep praying and keep loving, and never put the problem ahead of the person. Elder Matthew J. Eyring spoke on peace through the Holy Ghost and recalled giving a blessing to a father whose twin baby had died just before birth. Elder Michael A. Dunn described a friend who quietly carried his gear over the last 10 miles of a 100-mile race in 1998 and compared that to Christ's help.
item.dc:creator: KSL Staff

item.title: General conference special: 'Perpetual education: 25 years of hope and opportunity'
item.description: Student stories from the Philippines anchor KSL's general conference documentary on the Perpetual Education Fund, which the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints started 25 years ago. Students there describe how schooling paid for through the fund changed their prospects and their families' futures. Reporter Angie Denison's special credits the fund with reaching more than 135,000 people in over 80 countries. It casts education as a tool for ending poverty and for strengthening the communities graduates go on to serve.
item.dc:creator: Angie Denison, KSL

item.title: Utah State team launches data center initiative, initial survey shows most oppose them
item.description: Three out of four Utahns surveyed by Utah State University researchers, 75.4%, said they'd oppose or strongly oppose building a data center anywhere in the state, and resistance climbed sharply when the site would be near their homes. The roughly 900-person survey is the first product of Data Center Development in Utah, a grant-funded initiative of USU's Community and Natural Resources Institute led by professor Jessica Schad, who said the aim is local data for decision-makers. According to the report's executive summary, residents care most about water and energy use, chances for public input, and where and how big projects are. The team notes that the electricity data centers draw has its own water cost, and it plans county-level results for Cache, Box Elder and Millard plus policy analyses.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: Tennessee's prisons chief is resigning after failed execution of Christa Pike
item.description: Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee announced Saturday that Correction Commissioner Frank Strada will resign this month, days after a failed execution left Christa Pike unconscious and on a ventilator. Pike is now 50 and was sentenced to death for the 1995 torture-killing of classmate Colleen Slemmer. Her execution was stopped Wednesday after two doses of pentobarbital failed to kill her, and her lawyers believe a faulty IV sent the drug into tissue instead of a vein. It was Tennessee's second aborted execution since May, and Lee has paused executions and ordered an independent review, and Strada said leaving was best for the state while maintaining that staff followed protocol. Pike's attorneys called the failure systemic, and the AP notes Strada also oversaw troubled lethal injections in Arizona in 2022.
item.dc:creator: Ed White, Associated Press

item.title: Federal funding cuts lead to childcare subsidy reductions for thousands of Utah families
item.description: After losing more than $20 million in federal childcare money, Utah's Division of Workforce Services has cut subsidy eligibility for new applicants from 85% to 50% of state median income, reducing or ending help for thousands of families. The state estimates about 900 families, with roughly 1,500 children, will lose aid completely. Christina Robles, who runs four childcare centers where she says nearly every child is subsidized, puts the number of children affected in some way at more than 10,700. One of her clients, a Granite School District teacher with four children, no longer qualifies. Officials say restoring funding is up to the governor and Legislature, and Robles argued that pushing parents out of work will raise other public costs.
item.dc:creator: Debbie Worthen, KSL

item.title: Protein is everywhere. How much do you actually need?
item.description: With protein now marketed in everything from coffee to pretzels, Intermountain Health dietitian Sheila Patterson told KSL that the right amount varies with a person's weight, activity and goals. The 2025-2030 Dietary Guidelines suggest 1.2 to 1.6 grams per kilogram of body weight daily. Patterson recommends spreading that out at roughly 20 to 30 grams per meal rather than eating huge amounts at once, and she favors whole foods such as beans, lentils, nuts, seeds and lean meat over shakes and bars. She warned that chasing protein can crowd out fiber, carbohydrates and healthy fats. She said people on GLP-1 weight-loss drugs do need enough protein to keep muscle, but they also need balanced nutrition and fluids.
item.dc:creator: Emma Benson, KSL

item.title: Utah's childcare crisis: The increasing unaffordability and what's being done about it
item.description: KSL's Heather Peterson looks at why many Utah parents are questioning whether working still pays once daycare is covered. The median cost of licensed care for a child under 2 is about $1,180 a month, against a state median household income near $95,000. Jennifer Stout of Voices for Utah Children said families typically spend about 12% of their income on childcare, and single parents about 32%, far above the 7% national benchmark. A loss of roughly $21 million in federal money has pushed the state to tighten subsidy eligibility, and about 900 families are expected to lose aid entirely. Rep. Ashlee Matthews warned of a benefits cliff where a small raise costs families far more in support, and Sunshine Academy owner Linda Jo Sego, whose families mostly rely on subsidies, said providers and employers will feel the hit too.
item.dc:creator: Heather Peterson, KSL

item.title: General conference special: 'President Dallin H. Oaks: Defender of faith & freedom'
item.description: Dallin H. Oaks' path to leading the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, as its 18th president, is the subject of a KSL general conference documentary by Carole Mikita. Rather than focus on a single role, the program argues that defending faith, freedom and truth has tied together his years as a Supreme Court justice, a university president and an apostle. It frames the film as a tribute to his service, with attention to his testimony and teachings. It also considers the direction he may set for the church now that he leads it.
item.dc:creator: Carole Mikita, KSL

item.title: Japanese Fall Food Festival to share Japanese cuisine with Salt Lake City community
item.description: Takoyaki, okonomiyaki, gyoza, udon and sushi were on the menu Saturday as the Salt Lake Buddhist Temple held its Japanese Fall Food Festival, which temple president Troy Watanabe says raises more money than anything but the Obon Festival. The event grew out of a temple bazaar from the Japantown era, when Japanese American farmers gave part of their harvest to the temple and sold produce to the public. Watanabe recalled helping unload those crops as a boy. Food has always been the main draw, he said, and $20 parking came with a $20 food voucher.
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr, KSL

item.title: Saturday morning session: Summaries from Latter-day Saint general conference
item.description: KSL's live blog of the Saturday morning session of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints' 196th Semiannual General Conference summarized each talk, and the session opened with a vote to sustain church leaders. The session closed with President D. Todd Christofferson of the First Presidency calling gambling morally wrong. He singled out online sports betting, casino-style apps and prediction markets, and said young people are especially exposed. Bishop Sean Douglas of the Presiding Bishopric pointed to record numbers of missionaries and converts and urged young members not to let lesser options crowd out full-time missions. Elder Ulisses Soares spoke on the strength fasting brings, and the blog also included a glossary and links to the Spanish broadcast.
item.dc:creator: KSL Staff

item.title: Strong families don't just happen. Here's how experts say to build a family culture that lasts
item.description: A KSL NewsRadio "Inside Sources" special with hosts Holly Richardson and Greg Skordas argues that lasting family culture comes from small, repeated habits, not big trips or elaborate plans. Utah Office of Families director Alex Peterson described her household's nightly 10-minute cleanup that ends in a dance party and a weekly day without phones. She said cheap, ordinary rituals like shared dinners tell children they're secure and that they belong. FamilySearch Library operations manager Rachel Crump Matheus urged families to save stories, the hard ones too, perhaps by recording one memory a minute a day. Richardson, who has four biological children and 20 adopted from eight countries and has buried four daughters, said those stories teach kids resilience.
item.dc:creator: Andy Cupp, KSL

item.title: General conference special: 'Utah celebrates America 250'
item.description: Dan Rascon's KSL special for America's 250th anniversary follows the son of a Utah World War II airman to France, where they meet descendants of the family who sheltered his father after he was shot down. Before that, they stop in Duxford, England, where the Imperial War Museum now exhibits the airman's story. The program considers how that wartime protection still shapes both families. Other segments feature new citizens naturalized in Utah this year, anniversary service projects and the state's celebrations.
item.dc:creator: Dan Rascon, KSL

item.title: Swiss glaciers lose more than 5% of ice after record heatwave
item.description: A record European heat wave and a thin winter snowpack cost Switzerland's glaciers more than 5% of their ice this year, according to a report released Thursday by the GLAMOS monitoring network and the Swiss Academy of Sciences. Close to a fifth of the country's glacier ice has disappeared in the past five years. The Aletsch Glacier had its biggest melt on record, and the Tsanfleuron glacier thinned by more than four meters on average. GLAMOS director Matthias Huss said extreme melt years now come nearly every year, though 2026 did not top 2022. About 2.2 trillion liters of meltwater ran off between July and September, which eases summer droughts for now, but Huss said that buffer shrinks as the glaciers do.
item.dc:creator: Cecile Mantovani and Denis Balibouse, Reuters

item.title: KSL Truth Test: Fact-checking debate claims in Utah's 3rd Congressional District
item.description: KSL Investigators checked four claims from Friday's Utah Debate Commission matchup at Utah Tech University between Rep. Celeste Maloy, a Republican, and Democrat Kent Udell in the 3rd Congressional District. Maloy's statement that diesel prices are falling held up, since AAA shows a slight drop from September's record though prices remain far above last year. Her claim that debt-to-GDP fell last year for the first time in about 30 years was not accurate, because the ratio has fallen several times, including during the pandemic. Udell's claim that over 60% of the defense budget is unaccounted for was rated false, because the 64% figure auditors couldn't verify refers to budgetary resources, not annual spending. His charge that Maloy agreed aloud with Trump's description of the Bears Ears and Grand Staircase lands was also false, since recordings show it was deputy Interior Secretary Kate MacGregor who spoke.
item.dc:creator: Daniella Rivera and Daniel Woodruff, KSL

item.title: Animal welfare groups criticize response to bird flu outbreak at Utah mink farm
item.description: Animal Wellness Action, the Center for a Humane Economy and the Animal Welfare Institute are faulting Utah regulators for disclosing little about what advocates call the nation's first documented bird flu outbreak among farmed mink. The Utah Department of Agriculture and Food's records list seven confirmed cases in Salt Lake County mink in August, but the agency has cited the producer's privacy in declining to share details. Public records show the farm expected to lose about 80% of its animals, and officials placed only a "verbal hold" on the farm instead of a formal quarantine, and they told DHHS while human-transmission risk was studied. Department spokesman Leon Page said there is no U.S. playbook for the situation and that only Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins can approve a vaccine. Wayne Pacelle and Kate Dylewsky of the advocacy groups argued that mink farms can incubate dangerous mutations.
item.dc:creator: Alixel Cabrera, Utah News Dispatch

item.title: Utah colleges to implement 25 safety recommendations in the wake of Charlie Kirk's death
item.description: Utah's Board of Higher Education on Friday adopted 25 campus safety recommendations from a task force formed after Charlie Kirk was killed at Utah Valley University. Commissioner Geoffrey Landward said the shooting sped up work already underway and that the main goal is one shared set of policies for every public college and university. Under a common playbook, smaller campuses can borrow resources and form partnerships with larger ones. The measures include regular threat-assessment training for students, faculty and staff, more ways to report concerns, clearer emergency communication and tighter rules for event applications. Some take effect right away, and the rest phase in by the 2027-28 school year.
item.dc:creator: Heather Peterson, KSL

item.title: Beyond Silicon Slopes: Utah's next tech boom is getting physical
item.description: This KSL contributor piece argues that Utah's tech growth is moving from software toward "deep tech" built on hardware, such as drones, energy, aerospace, advanced manufacturing and quantum work. Vector co-founder Andy Yakulis said the defense firm picked Utah over Virginia, California and Austin for its engineers, military bases and nearby open land. That land lets the company test-fly drones minutes from its Bluffdale factory, and he said investors have only warmed to hardware in the past five years or so. In Emery County, state energy director Emy Lesofski described the Utah San Rafael Energy Lab as shared testing space for startups, where Valar Atomics' Ward 250 reactor reached criticality in June, the first DOE-authorized reactor built outside a national lab. Nucleus Institute CEO Jefferson Moss said what's new is the scale, the money, and these industries starting to overlap.
item.dc:creator: Brooke Nally for KSL

item.title: Utah State Fairpark warns of scam targeting food vendors
item.description: The Utah State Fairpark says scammers posing as its staff have used calls, fake applications and lookalike email addresses to tell food vendors they've been booked for events and then demand payment, and some vendors have lost thousands of dollars. Deputy executive director Nicki Claeys said reports came in around the Utah State Fair and again ahead of the RedWest music festival, though the Fairpark doesn't know the total losses. She stressed that the Fairpark always signs a contract and never asks for money up front. Genuine staff emails end in @utahstatefair.com. Vendors can check any offer by calling 801-538-8400, and victims should report it to the Fairpark and police.
item.dc:creator: Emma Benson, KSL

item.title: Woman upset with divorce illegally accesses her attorney's computer
item.description: Amber Lynn Cherrington, 52, of West Jordan, was charged Friday in 3rd District Court with eight counts of unlawful computer access and one count of stalking. Prosecutors say that in February 2025 her former divorce attorney, worn down by months of unannounced visits and demands, let her use the attorney's e-filing login to look at her own case. Charges say she instead opened many other clients' confidential files, which went unnoticed until May 2026. She allegedly emailed those records, with personal identifying information, to several groups of people and bragged about the access in online reviews meant to hurt the firm. Investigators are also looking into emails sent to TV stations in the attorney's husband's name falsely warning of a mass shooting.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Cyclospora found at Mexican farm linked to lettuce outbreak, FDA says
item.description: The FDA said Friday that its inspectors found cyclospora in a wastewater tank and a drainage ditch at the Taylor Farms lettuce site in Guanajuato, Mexico, which was tied to the biggest U.S. outbreak of the parasite on record. Though the outbreak caused close to 13,000 illnesses, the agency still can't say how the contamination happened, but it called the link strong and closed its investigation. The inspection was its first visit to the farm in more than seven years, after foreign food-safety inspections dropped off following the pandemic. Taylor Farms blamed an independent grower it has since dropped and said its Mexico facility will stay closed while it tightens safety. Mexican regulators found no parasite earlier, and the FDA had to retract a mistaken border test.
item.dc:creator: Matthew Perrone, Associated Press

item.title: New visitor and learning center opens at Antelope Island State Park
item.description: Antelope Island State Park opened its new visitor and learning center to the public Friday after two years of construction, replacing a 500-square-foot building with a 33,000-square-foot complex. Interactive exhibits cover the Great Salt Lake, brine shrimp, geology, wildlife, dark skies and the island's Indigenous ties, and the building adds two classrooms, two conference rooms, a larger gift shop and the 200-plus-seat Larry H. and Gail Miller Family Theater, which screens "Secrets of Great Salt Lake" and the Northwestern Band of the Shoshone Nation's "Keepers of Water." Park manager Doranne Pittz said the design was meant to blend into the landscape and that the classrooms finally give the thousands of visiting school groups an indoor home base. Bird photographer Norman Kikuchi, a regular, said the center brings nature to people who rarely get outside, and many visitors will see it first at the Oct. 24 bison roundup.
item.dc:creator: Alex Cabrero, KSL

item.title: Logan man who fled from police after domestic violence response pleads guilty
item.description: Antonio Zarco-Orozco, 40, of Logan, who police first sought under the name Benigno Queredo-Centreros, pleaded guilty Monday to reduced charges of theft, aggravated assault, domestic violence in the presence of a child and leaving the scene of an injury crash, with nine other counts, including aggravated kidnapping, dismissed. Charges say that on July 13 he shoved his longtime girlfriend into a bookshelf and choked her with his forearm until she got her phone's voice assistant to dial 911, then took her truck. Police say he hit 107 mph on state Route 30, struck a car and injured two people, and fled on foot with a long gun toward Benson Marina, likely swimming across before officers could close a perimeter. He was arrested in Tremonton a week later and is due for sentencing Nov. 9; court records show prior assault and domestic violence convictions in 2005 and 2009.
item.dc:creator: Cassidy Wixom, KSL

item.title: Salt Lake City's Donner Trail Park gets major makeover
item.description: Salt Lake City finished a four-month overhaul of Donner Trail Park on Thursday, adding playgrounds, water-wise landscaping, a walking path and a Memorial Tree Grove of 83 trees across 17 species. Residents can now reserve a grove tree online for a $380 donation to honor a person, group or historic moment, with the first plantings set for spring 2027, urban forester Tony Gliot said. The park also debuts "Journey Lines," 16 stone and steel pieces by artist Adam Kuby that evoke canyon and mountain routes, the first art paid for by the city's parks bond. The bond covered $870,000 of the work, and the grove got another $434,000 in capital improvement funds.
item.dc:creator: Tyrese Boone, KSL

item.title: Bicyclist dies in Kaysville crash
item.description: Kaysville police say a 70-year-old man riding a bicycle was killed Friday afternoon when he and a vehicle collided near Main Street and Nicholls Road. The crash was reported around 4:05 p.m., and the cyclist died at the scene despite paramedics' efforts. Police closed southbound Main Street at Burton Lane into the evening and asked drivers to detour.
item.dc:creator: Payton Davis, KSL

item.title: Watch live: Celeste Maloy, Kent Udell take debate stage in 3rd Congressional District race
item.description: Republican Rep. Celeste Maloy and Democratic challenger Kent Udell were scheduled to debate Friday at 6 p.m. at Utah Tech University's Eccles Fine Arts Center in St. George in the race for Utah's newly drawn 3rd Congressional District. Maloy, who now represents the 2nd District, is seeking a second full term, while Udell, an engineer and academic, is a first-time candidate.
