A Utah Debate Commission poll showed Maloy at nearly 45% and Udell at 26%, both above the 10% bar to qualify, while Constitution, Libertarian and two independent candidates missed the cut. KSL carried the debate live about a month before Election Day.
item.dc:creator: Bridger Beal-Cvetko, KSL

item.title: Here's what happens to abandoned property found along Utah highways
item.description: Utah Highway Patrol Lt. Jalaine Hawkes says drivers who lose something off a roof rack or out of a truck bed should call the Department of Public Safety, because troopers patrol around the clock and know where debris tends to land. A rough idea of where the item went missing helps, she said, and most roadside finds are trash, though troopers have turned up surprises such as a firearm. The most rewarding returns, she said, are children's stuffed animals and toys. The department tries to reach owners of anything with a name or serial number, while unidentifiable items are usually discarded after 10 days.
item.dc:creator: Cameron Elliott and Wendy Leonard, KSL

item.title: Salt Lake police arrest man in shooting investigation
item.description: Salt Lake City police on Thursday arrested Wilber Alexander Diaz Orosco, 28, on suspicion of firing a gun during an Aug. 31 confrontation near 650 W. South Temple and possessing a firearm as a restricted person. An officer nearby heard shots, watched one car slam into another and then race toward him amid more gunfire, and chased the fleeing Nissan to City Creek property, where its two occupants were caught after running. Those men told detectives someone in the car they struck had shot at them first, and a witness backed that account; officers found a .38-caliber pistol and two casings at the scene. License plate readers led detectives to Diaz, whom they watched for weeks, and police say he is in the country illegally and has had prior immigration arrests.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: 'Kingdom of Faith': History of the Church of Jesus Christ in Cambodia featured in documentary
item.description: A KSL documentary, "Kingdom of Faith: The Saints in Cambodia," traces how The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints went from official recognition in Cambodia in February 1994 to a dedicated temple in Phnom Penh this August. Much of the opening credit goes to Vichit Ith, who escaped the country as a teenager before the Khmer Rouge took power and returned in 1993 with then-Thailand Bangkok Mission President Larry White; his later post as an economic adviser to the new prime minister helped clear the way. The film also follows the Eav family, who survived the Khmer Rouge years, walked through mined jungle to a Thai refugee camp, and rebuilt in Seattle, and who now have five grandchildren called as missionaries to Cambodia and grandparents serving in the new temple's presidency. The church reports nearly 18,000 members there, and the program airs Oct. 4 at 12:30 p.m. between general conference sessions.
item.dc:creator: Keri Wilcox, KSL

item.title: Man sentenced to jail, probation after police say he brandished stolen gun at another driver
item.description: Travis Lorenz, 21, of West Jordan received three years of probation and credit for 101 days already served after pleading guilty to a reduced third-degree felony charge of possessing a gun he should have known was stolen; an aggravated assault charge was dropped. Charging documents say Lorenz threw something at another car during a road rage encounter, pulled alongside and displayed a handgun while telling the driver to use a turn signal, and later admitted he bought the gun from a drug dealer. Third District Judge Derek Williams suspended a prison term of up to five years at the Sept. 17 sentencing. Lorenz also pleaded guilty in a separate 4th District case to misdemeanor assault with substantial bodily injury and received two more years of probation.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: US court trims Joby's trade-secret case against Archer Aviation
item.description: A federal judge in Northern California has thrown out part of Joby Aero's trade-secret and contract case against fellow air-taxi developer Archer Aviation in a Sept. 29 ruling that also dismissed Archer's counterclaims, Archer said Friday. Joby's 2025 lawsuit claims former policy lead George Kivork emailed dozens of company files to himself and changed access permissions on hundreds more before moving to Archer, which Joby says then used the information to undercut a deal with a real-estate developer. The case continues on the remaining claims, with Joby seeking damages and an injunction. It is one of several legal fights in the emerging electric air-taxi industry, including Archer's 2023 settlement with Boeing-owned Wisk.
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: Disney licenses lineup of movies, TV shows to Netflix including 'Ice Age,' 'Will Trent'
item.description: Disney is licensing a package of films and series to Netflix, starting Oct. 4 with the first two seasons of the Disney+ show "Percy Jackson and the Olympians" and all five "Ice Age" movies, each streaming worldwide for three months. The "Ice Age" window precedes next year's theatrical release of "Ice Age: Boiling Point," and "Will Trent" is also part of the deal. Disney and Pixar titles including "Soul," "Elio" and "Raya and the Last Dragon" are set to follow in early 2027 on varying regional schedules. Disney said most of its branded content will stay exclusive to its own platforms, while Netflix continues adding licensed libraries such as AMC's "The Walking Dead."
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: 'Transformational opportunity': Snow College gets $3M federal grant to lead Utah's rural AI future
item.description: Snow College has won a $3 million federal grant, among the largest in its recent history, to create a Center for Rural AI Adoption and Integration as part of a five-year initiative. The money first gives students, faculty and staff at the Ephraim, Richfield and Nephi campuses enterprise-grade AI tools and works AI literacy into coursework, then extends training through the college's rural concurrent enrollment network to hundreds of high school students and teachers each year. Provost Michael Austin called it a "transformational opportunity" to make sure small-town Utah is not left out of the shift. The grant arrives alongside Gov. Spencer Cox's $5 million Utah AI Moonshot research program launched in August.
item.dc:creator: Logan Stefanich, KSL

item.title: FDA closes lettuce parasite probe, links outbreak to Mexico facility
item.description: The FDA has wrapped up its investigation into this summer's multistate cyclospora outbreak, tying the illnesses to recalled shredded iceberg lettuce from Taylor Farms de Mexico. Inspectors found the parasite in a wastewater tank at the company's processing plant and in a drainage ditch at a lettuce grower identified through traceback, though the agency could not determine exactly how the contamination occurred. The CDC, which declared the outbreak over Sept. 11, logged 19,883 lab-confirmed cases and two deaths. The FDA also laid out a 10-point prevention plan for the 2027 growing season, including more monitoring of high-risk produce and outreach to growers.
item.dc:creator: Kamal Choudhury, Reuters

item.title: Amazon to invest $1B into data center communities amid backlash against data center rollouts
item.description: Amazon says it will put more than $1 billion over five years into towns that host its data centers, funding job training, education, water and energy conservation and other local projects, on top of about $1 billion it says it spent in such places over the last three years. In a Friday blog post, AWS chief Matt Garman also said the company has stopped using nondisclosure agreements with government partners, and he warned that the more than 100 local moratoriums under consideration could cost the U.S. the AI race. The move comes as data centers become a midterm campaign issue, with polling showing about 6 in 10 Americans favor limits on new construction and many worry about power bills and water. Amazon has raised its 2026 capital spending forecast to $220 billion.
item.dc:creator: Anne D'innocenzio, Associated Press

item.title: Christa Pike was on ventilator and unconscious after failed Tennessee execution, attorneys say
item.description: Attorneys for Christa Pike told a court Friday that she was unconscious and on a ventilator in a hospital after Tennessee's attempt to execute her failed Wednesday, with staff working to flush two doses of pentobarbital from her system. Her lawyers believe misplaced IV lines or blown veins sent the drug into her tissue rather than her bloodstream, and that the team gave a backup dose without catching the problem; defense attorney Randy Spivey counted at least seven needle sites on her arm during the hourlong effort. The state has not explained what went wrong. Gov. Bill Lee ordered an independent review and indefinitely postponed Pike's execution and another set for this year, and some Republican leaders want the single-drug method reconsidered.
item.dc:creator: Kim Chandler and Jamie Stengle, Associated Press

item.title: Gov. Cox, first lady Abby Cox kick off statewide reading across Utah
item.description: Gov. Spencer Cox and first lady Abby Cox opened the Utah Reads Read-a-Thon on Friday with nearly 500 students reading on blankets in the Capitol rotunda, while schools, libraries and universities statewide joined in throughout the day. Abby Cox said the goal is to get children off screens and into books, noting that reading rates in Utah and nationally are not where they should be. Many students named fantasy series such as "Fablehaven" and "Keeper of the Lost Cities" as favorites, and parents said the Capitol backdrop made the hour feel special. Organizers hope the one-day event builds reading habits that last.
item.dc:creator: Annette Campbell, KSL

item.title: 3 Utahns federally charged, accused of robbing credit union with hoax explosive
item.description: A federal grand jury on Wednesday indicted Thomas Domingo Bustos, 31, of Layton; Brelyn Sanchez, 37, of Ogden; and Fidel Ybarra, 52, of Riverdale on credit union robbery and hoax charges tied to a Sept. 4 holdup in South Salt Lake. Prosecutors say Ybarra handed a teller at an America First Credit Union on State Street a note and showed a fake bomb built from fireworks and duct tape, leaving with $1,234, while Sanchez drove the getaway car and a second vehicle registered to Bustos trailed them. Ybarra told police Bustos had threatened him and his family over a $19,000 casino loss in Wendover and ordered the robbery to settle the debt, then kept the cash. Bustos, described in charging papers as having a violent record and documented gang ties, is accused of making the device and dictating the note.
item.dc:creator: Cassidy Wixom, KSL

item.title: Kennedy Center Honors to be held at Capital One Arena amid fight over adding Trump's name
item.description: The 49th Kennedy Center Honors will be staged Dec. 7 at Washington's Capital One Arena rather than at the Kennedy Center, which its board voted last month to close after a judge blocked putting President Donald Trump's name back on the building. A center spokesperson gave no reason for the venue change and said this year's honorees will be named later. Trump has said the building needs safety repairs but tied them to adding his name, while a federal judge has ruled twice that only Congress, which set aside $257 million for repairs, can authorize a renaming. The 1964 law creating the center as a memorial to John F. Kennedy bars the board from naming it for anyone else.
item.dc:creator: Mike Catalini, Associated Press

item.title: $6K reward offered after elk shot, left for dead at private farm
item.description: The Utah Department of Agriculture and Food and the owners of Valley View Elk Farm near Monroe are offering $6,000 for information on who shot a young bull elk on the private Sevier County farm. Todd Gardner first assumed the roughly 3-year-old animal died naturally before finding a bullet wound, and sheriff's deputies recovered fragments. Stuart Barney of the state's domestic elk program said the elk could have been worth $10,000 to $17,000 at maturity and that he could not recall a similar shooting on an elk farm in at least seven years. Wren Gardner appealed online for tips, and anyone with information can contact the Sevier County Sheriff's Office, Richfield police or the agriculture department.
item.dc:creator: Randall Jeppesen and Joe R. Wirthlin Jr, KSL

item.title: David Ellison says combined Paramount and Warner Bros Discovery will be named Skydance
item.description: David Ellison said the company formed by Paramount Skydance's $110 billion takeover of Warner Bros Discovery will be called Skydance, arguing a fresh corporate name lets the Paramount and Warner Bros studio brands keep top billing. A regulatory filing shows the legal name change taking effect Oct. 6, when the Class B shares are also expected to move from Nasdaq to the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker SKYD. The announcement follows a federal judge's order this week clearing the deal after a settlement with 12 states led by California, and Ellison's naming of Mattel chief Ynon Kreiz as co-CEO to run integration. Emarketer analyst Ross Benes called the choice "ego-driven," and the combined company is targeting $6 billion in savings while carrying about $80 billion in debt.
item.dc:creator: Anzar Mehraj, Reuters

item.title: DA proposes civil commitment court during mental health symposium
item.description: Salt Lake County District Attorney Sim Gill used his third Criminal Justice and Mental Health Symposium on Friday to float a dedicated civil commitment court, modeled on Utah's mental health and drug courts, for people with severe mental illness who refuse voluntary treatment. Gill argued the criminal justice system has become the default mental health provider and is filled with people neither competent for trial nor functionally capable, while most involuntary commitments last only 72 hours. He cited Utah's 8.4 psychiatric beds per 100,000 residents against a recommended 40 to 60, and said untreated illness worsens until early intervention no longer works. Advocates Debra Widmer of the Utah Shattering Silence Coalition and Sherri Wittwer of the Utah Coalition for Severe Mental Illness, which co-sponsored the event, called for treating these illnesses medically rather than through jails.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: 'Extraordinary generosity': Church of Jesus Christ donates over $7M to the American Red Cross
item.description: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints is giving the American Red Cross $7.047 million, including nearly $3 million for blood services and equipment, $2 million for the Red Cross Sickle Cell Initiative, and $710,000 to enlarge its blood lab in Murray, plus 50 collection machines and four emergency vehicles. A separate $850,000 goes to recovery from April's Super Typhoon Sinlaku in Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands. Church members give about 97,000 units of blood a year, and church-hosted drives have produced more than 1 million units since the first one in 1996, making the church the Red Cross's largest blood drive partner. Presiding Bishop W. Christopher Waddell and Red Cross CEO Cliff Holtz both commented on the gift, which follows $5.1 million in 2025 and $7.35 million in 2024.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: Swedish ball-bearing ad revives Greta Garbo with US, Chinese AI
item.description: Swedish ball-bearing maker SKF has released an ad starring an AI re-creation of Greta Garbo, who appeared in a promotional film for the company more than a century ago and died in 1990. SKF communications chief Per Nilsson said copyright limits meant the likeness was built from text prompts rather than archival images, using ByteDance, Google and Kuaishou tools, while the voice was trained on one licensed early film with help from a human actor for timing. The company said it worked with Garbo's estate and family and called the result respectful. Critics were less kind: The Guardian's Peter Bradshaw gave it one star, AI researcher Henry Ajder called it "synthetic resurrection," and George Clooney recently said he hoped never to turn up in a tampon ad after his death.
item.dc:creator: Ilze Filks, Francesca Halliwell and Greta Rosen Fondahn, Reuters

item.title: G7 nations agree to release 100 million barrels of oil, including diesel, a boost for Trump
item.description: G7 nations agreed Friday to a 100 million-barrel coordinated oil release over four months through the International Energy Agency, with a large share of diesel delivered in the first 20 days. The step followed an overnight call between President Donald Trump and French President Emmanuel Macron, who chairs the group, and a Macron-led video meeting of leaders. U.S. diesel averaged $6.37 a gallon on Friday after a record $6.52 on Sept. 22, according to AAA, as the eight-month Iran war keeps fuel prices high. The relief comes as Trump faces sagging economic approval ahead of November's midterms, with an AP-NORC poll finding most adults blame him for rising prices.
item.dc:creator: Collin Binkley, Associated Press

item.title: 'Kind of crazy': Mortgage rates soar, hurting housing affordability
item.description: Freddie Mac's average 30-year fixed mortgage rate has climbed to 7.28% after its steepest weekly jump since October 2022, and mortgage applications fell 6% in a week, according to the Mortgage Bankers Association. BYU economist Christian vom Lehn said rates are about a point higher than a year ago because of inflation, economic expectations and the Iran war's push on energy costs, and he expects the result to be slower price growth rather than a big drop from Utah's $520,000 median. Provo townhome owners Christian and Sadie Hawkins, who locked in at 5.3% two years ago, said that rate felt high then but now looks lucky, and they have shelved plans to buy again until rates ease.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Woodruff, KSL

item.title: Respiratory virus season has arrived. Flu, COVID-19 and RSV vaccines are available
item.description: Flu, COVID-19 and RSV shots are now stocked at most major pharmacies, and with the CDC simply reposting last year's guidance after upheaval on its vaccine advisory panel, medical societies have issued their own 2026-27 recommendations built on independent reviews by the AMA and the Vaccine Integrity Project. The groups advise annual flu shots for everyone 6 months and up, enhanced doses for those 65 and older, and a newly available mRNA flu vaccine for adults over 50, with October cited as the ideal time to get one. A single, non-annual RSV dose is advised for everyone over 75 and for high-risk adults 50 and older, along with maternal vaccination at 32 to 36 weeks or antibodies for young infants, and the groups say all adults should get an updated COVID-19 shot. American Academy of Family Physicians President Dr. Sarah Nosal said insurers have indicated they will cover the shots, and the Vaccine Integrity Project's Dr. Bruce Gellin said the breakdown in the federal process must not leave a gap in guidance.
item.dc:creator: Jacqueline Howard, CNN

item.title: Utah man's exploitation of Texas teen was 'shock to the conscience,' police say
item.description: Cameron Joe Boyer, a 50-year-old from Pleasant Grove, was booked into the Utah County Jail on Thursday on allegations including aggravated sexual exploitation of a minor and enticing a minor, stemming from online contact with a 17-year-old in Texas. The case began in 2024 after the girl told a teacher about an unmoderated chat site where, according to a police affidavit, Boyer said he was interested in underage girls and claimed to have explicit images of other Utah children. Investigators say warrants on his accounts turned up degrading instructions he gave the teen, threats to share her pictures, and a long Snapchat history with other minors. The arresting officer described the material as a "shock to the conscience."
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Polish city reopens Cold War shelter as Russian attacks in Ukraine intensify
item.description: With Russian strikes on western Ukraine drawing nearer to Poland, Lublin has modernized a mid-1980s air raid shelter beneath its municipal bus company, and its emergency exit now points west instead of east. MPK Lublin civil defense inspector Kamil Rzad said it can keep 200 people for up to 72 hours on independent air, water and power. Nationwide, the government counts about 2,000 shelters for roughly 300,000 people plus more than 86,000 lesser refuges such as basements and garages, yet some residents, including 77-year-old Elzbieta Woznica, admit they have no idea where they would go. Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Polish jets are now scrambled day and night as Russian attacks near the border become routine.
item.dc:creator: Anna Koper and Kuba Stezycki, Reuters

item.title: Nurse, fellow hikers help save man's life after cardiac arrest on Big Cottonwood Canyon trail
item.description: Bystanders kept up CPR on a 67-year-old Argentine visitor, identified only as Ricardo, for as long as half an hour after he went into cardiac arrest on a Big Cottonwood Canyon trail, and he had a pulse again by the time rescuers carried him out. Miley Feltman, a University of Utah nurse, was the first to start compressions after the man collapsed just as she and her partner were backing away from a moose and calf; two other hikers joined so the three could trade off. Unified Fire Authority and Salt Lake County Search and Rescue crews needed 20 to 30 minutes to reach the remote spot. Unified Fire spokesman Nate Cochran said backcountry emergencies are hard because help and other people are scarce, and both he and Feltman urged the public to learn hands-only CPR.
item.dc:creator: Annette Campbell, KSL

item.title: A trail near Moab could help shape the future of accessible public lands
item.description: The Bureau of Land Management picked Moab's Lions Park on National Public Lands Day to launch All Americans Outside, a national push to make its 245 million acres easier to enjoy for people with disabilities, veterans and others. BLM Director Steve Pearce said the idea grew out of a Grand Junction roundtable with Interior Secretary Doug Burgum and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy on nature's health benefits, and that his brother's lifelong wheelchair use made the cause personal. Acting Utah BLM Director Christina Price steered the ceremony to Moab because of the Colorado River Gap Trail Project, a paved multi-use path along state Route 128 being extended 0.7 miles to roughly 2.5 miles in all. Each state is being asked to stand up at least three accessible sites soon, and the Outdoor Recreation Roundtable's Jessica Turner endorsed the effort. The Deseret News report was republished by KSL.
item.dc:creator: Kevin Lind, Deseret News

item.title: Astronauts arrive at International Space Station on the quickest US express flight yet
item.description: SpaceX's Crew-13 reached the International Space Station about eight hours after liftoff from Cape Canaveral on Thursday, the fastest trip any U.S. spacecraft has made to the outpost, thanks to the station's favorable position at launch. Commander Jessica Watkins, a geologist on her second station mission, became the first Black woman to command a crew to orbit; first-time flyers NASA's Luke Delaney, Canada's Joshua Kutryk and Russia's Sergey Teteryatnikov round out the team, which launched after a three-week delay to repair a fuel leak. The crew leaned into its Apollo 13 nod with "Lucky 13" plates and a crocheted good-luck dragon. Kutryk's wife is due with their third child in late November, making him the fourth man to become a father in orbit during a six-month stay.
item.dc:creator: Marcia Dunn, Associated Press

item.title: DNA evidence from Thomas Jefferson's hair reveals the truth about his relationship with Sally Hemings
item.description: New genetic work led by Smithsonian scholar Richard Kurin puts the probability that Thomas Jefferson fathered at least one of Sally Hemings' children at 99.96%, the strongest evidence yet in a 200-year-old debate. The project started with a reddish-blond hair found in a Jefferson Bible in 2011, which turned out not to be his, but Monticello later supplied verified locks, including one cut at his deathbed, that let researchers compare his reconstructed genome with DNA from 16 living people descended from several branches, including Hemings' sons Eston and Madison. Unlike the 1998 Y-chromosome study, which could link Hemings' descendants only to some Jefferson male, this work used the president's own DNA. Kurin describes the effort in a new book, "History by a Hair," and a preprint not yet peer-reviewed, and outside geneticist Éadaoin Harney said the approach could help reconnect descendants of poorly documented enslaved people.
item.dc:creator: Mindy Weisberger, CNN

item.title: Easy-to-guess passwords have cybersecurity experts clamoring for an evolution
item.description: An Alan Boswell Group review of breach data from Have I Been Pwned found people still lean on painfully guessable passwords, with "123456" showing up nearly 210 million times and "password," "admin" and "qwerty" each in the tens of millions. Personal choices are not much safer: Daniel led among names, Liverpool among teams and Superman among characters, while nearly 4 million accounts used "monkey." The firm's Heath Alexander-Bew said those strings already sit in leaked lists that attackers try automatically, and he recommended blocking common passwords, turning on multi-factor authentication and using a password manager. Kathryn Linford of Insight IT told the KSL Investigators that passwords are becoming obsolete and that passkeys, biometrics and trusted devices will likely take their place.
item.dc:creator: Matt Gephardt and Sloan Schrage, KSL

item.title: 'More than just a fabric shop:' Granny's Fabric House provides a quilting community for everyone
item.description: Vanessa Johnson opened Granny's Fabric House on Main Street in Rexburg in June 2022, sharing the storefront with the Idaho Sewing Center, and the shop has outgrown and moved spaces three times. Johnson, who taught herself to quilt from YouTube videos about seven years ago, says she wanted to fill a gap in local quilting supplies and build a welcoming community. The shop hosts open sew nights, evening Sip N Sew gatherings, embroidery and bag-making classes, and a monthly charity sewing day benefiting a different local cause each time. She also finishes unfinished heirloom quilt tops that customers bring in. The profile is from East Idaho News reporter Andrea Olson.
item.dc:creator: Andrea Olson, East Idaho News

item.title: Moderna to replace Warner Bros Discovery on Nasdaq 100
item.description: Index changes driven by the Warner Bros. Discovery-Paramount Skydance merger are opening a Nasdaq 100 spot for Moderna, whose shares have climbed more than sixfold in 2026. Moderna, now worth roughly $75 billion, joins the index Oct. 9, according to a Nasdaq announcement reported by Reuters. The long-delayed media merger is expected to close days earlier, prompting other index providers to drop Warner Bros. Discovery too.
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: Proposed amendment would raise the bar for some Utah ballot initiatives
item.description: Amendment B on Utah's November ballot would require any citizen initiative that creates or raises taxes to win at least 60% of the vote. Sponsors Sen. Lincoln Fillmore and Rep. Jason Kyle say a tax increase imposed by initiative should have broad support, since voters cannot hold each other accountable the way they can lawmakers. The opposition campaign Utahns Protecting Our Constitution, with Better Boundaries director Elizabeth Rasmussen, calls it a permanent weakening of the initiative process, noting that 2018 measures legalizing medical marijuana and expanding Medicaid would have failed under the new bar. A Noble Predictive Insights poll last month found 50% support and 21% opposition, and opponents are planning TV ads, mailers and canvassing before the Nov. 3 election.
item.dc:creator: Bridger Beal-Cvetko, KSL

item.title: Hiker hospitalized after falling estimated 100 feet in Iron County
item.description: A medical helicopter carried a 20-year-old woman to the hospital Thursday morning after she fell roughly 100 feet off a mountainside at Red Hollow, near state Route 14 east of Cedar City. Iron County deputies needed help from search and rescue volunteers and a ropes team to reach her in the steep terrain. She had a head injury and was disoriented, according to the sheriff's office, which noted the area's growing popularity with students looking for sunrise views and cautioned against hiking near cliffs before daylight.
item.dc:creator: Devin Oldroyd, KSL

item.title: Third aircraft carrier and thousands of troops head to Mideast as Trump weighs new Iran strikes
item.description: About 9,000 U.S. sailors and Marines are heading to the Middle East with the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier group and the USS Makin Island amphibious group, which could put three carriers in the region by late October, a U.S. official told the Associated Press. President Donald Trump said early indications tie Iran to the FlyDubai co-pilot who attacked his captain and tried to crash an Israel-bound flight, and promised a heavy response if confirmed. In a Time interview, Trump said more bombing after the Nov. 3 elections is possible and that he rejected Iran's latest ceasefire offer as inadequate. British authorities separately arrested a dual U.K.-Iranian national over an alleged plot linked to a security incident near RAF Fairford, a base U.S. bombers have used against Iran.
item.dc:creator: Konstantin Toropin, Michelle L. Price and Aamer Madhani, Associated Press

item.title: In China's Taoist martial arts schools, fighting is only part of the lesson
item.description: At his kung fu academy in China's Wudang Mountains, founded in 2004, master Yuan Shimao teaches that martial arts are as much about inner stillness and Taoist philosophy as punching and kicking. Yuan, who came to Wudang in the late 1980s hoping Taoist practice would ease his rheumatism, now runs a five-year training course, a wellness program for adults and a summer camp for children, and says his students are getting younger. Wudang Museum's Shu Chenghai explains the mountain's long religious history, student Guo Xinyi describes tai chi helping her defuse family conflict, and American Jake Pinnick, who arrived at 20, has spent 16 years there and opened his own academy. Yuan says his teaching has dropped corporal punishment and harsh training in favor of motivating chants. The report is from the Associated Press.
item.dc:creator: María Teresa Hernández, Associated Press

item.title: Tokyo court grants legal protection to human voices in AI clone case
item.description: In a first for Japan, the Tokyo District Court on Wednesday recognized legal protection for a person's voice, siding with anime voice actor Kenjiro Tsuda against the operator of a TikTok account that used an AI imitation of his voice. The anonymous account, which had more than 200,000 subscribers, narrated over 180 urban-legend videos in a voice resembling Tsuda's, known for playing Kento Nanami in "Jujutsu Kaisen." Presiding Judge Aya Takahashi compared a voice to a portrait and found its unauthorized commercial use violated publicity rights, though she did not order the videos removed because the account was already gone. The ruling comes as Japanese voice actors grow increasingly worried about AI cloning, the Associated Press reports.
item.dc:creator: Mari Yamaguchi, Associated Press

item.title: Failed Tennessee execution raises questions about Utah's lethal injection protocol
item.description: Tennessee's failed attempt to execute Christa Pike, who survived two doses of pentobarbital Wednesday night, has raised questions about how Utah would handle a similar situation. Salt Lake City attorney Greg Skordas said Tennessee could legally try again, but a repeated attempt could be challenged as cruel and unusual punishment under the Eighth Amendment, and he expects states using lethal injection to revisit their protocols. Utah's execution policy includes backup drug doses but does not spell out what happens if several doses fail, and Department of Corrections spokesman Richard Piatt said much of the policy is kept confidential for security. Pike, sentenced for the 1995 killing of Colleen Slemmer, remains on death row while Tennessee officials decide how to proceed.
item.dc:creator: Annette Campbell, KSL

item.title: Utah County to 'expand the healing' for domestic violence survivors with new safehaven
item.description: The Refuge Utah, a domestic violence shelter and rape crisis center, broke ground Thursday in Orem on a 34,000-square-foot Utah County campus that will grow its emergency shelter from 25 beds to 138. Later phases will add a 12,000-square-foot advocacy and services center and transitional family housing; the group has raised more than $13 million toward a $35 million goal. Capital campaign chair Mary Crafts said 740 women and children were turned away last year because of lack of space. Board member Lyndsey Hackford, a former shelter resident, joined Executive Director Ashlee Taylor, Orem Mayor Karen McCandless and Rep. Tyler Clancy at the event, held on the first day of Domestic Violence Awareness Month.
item.dc:creator: Cassidy Wixom, KSL

item.title: 5-year-old may be youngest to ever DJ a music festival
item.description: Hadley Lovell, a 5-year-old kindergartner at South Jordan's Monte Vista Elementary, DJ'd a schoolwide assembly Thursday marking Utah's Read-a-Thon. She and her older brother Carter picked up the hobby after their father, assistant principal Andrew Lovell, bought a used DJ deck, and their videos now have more than 175,000 Instagram followers. The family has submitted Hadley's recent set at an electronic dance music festival to Guinness World Records as a possible record for the youngest female festival DJ. Her father said his proudest moment was seeing her refuse to leave the stage after a mistake and finish the set while the crowd cheered.
item.dc:creator: Alex Cabrero, KSL

item.title: Nike plans more job cuts to boost sputtering turnaround, forecasts steep revenue drop
item.description: Nike shares dropped 8.5% after hours Thursday when the company forecast a high-single-digit fall in fiscal 2027 revenue, far worse than the roughly 2% decline analysts expected, and announced more job cuts. CEO Elliott Hill's restructuring will reduce Nike to three geographic regions, open a new campus in India and save about $2.5 billion through fiscal 2031; the number of layoffs is not yet known, with notifications starting in 2027. First-quarter sales fell about 4% to $11.21 billion, missing estimates, and China sales dropped 26% in constant currency for a ninth straight quarterly decline, while North America grew 2%. Analysts quoted by Reuters questioned whether Nike's China troubles are about products rather than sales channels.
item.dc:creator: Danielle Kaye and Angela Christy M, Reuters

item.title: Lighting and sound teams help General Conference messages spread throughout the world
item.description: A church-produced video ahead of the 196th Semiannual General Conference shows the audio and lighting crews who prepare the Conference Center in Salt Lake City. Technicians check roughly 900 to 1,100 light fixtures and more than 500 speakers across the 21,000-seat hall, swap out the lights before every conference, and work from two miles of catwalks overhead. Lead audio engineer Aaron Kobel, lighting specialist Braden Earl Howard and broadcast producer Jody Hadfield describe the work as a spiritual effort to keep distractions away from the messages. Sessions run at 10 a.m. and 2 p.m. Saturday and Sunday, with broadcasts on church apps, KSL TV, KSL NewsRadio and KSL.com.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: Comcast's NBCUniversal cuts streaming technology jobs
item.description: Comcast's Sky unit in Europe will bear most of a new round of NBCUniversal layoffs aimed at its global streaming technology group, a source told Reuters, with a smaller number of U.S. roles also affected. How many jobs go will depend on consultations with staff. NBCUniversal framed the proposal as positioning the group for growth, part of a broader industry effort to make streaming profitable after heavy spending.
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: Utah State University to join statewide Read-a-Thon Friday
item.description: Utah State University is asking its students, faculty and staff to set aside an hour for Gov. Spencer Cox and First Lady Abby Cox's statewide Read-a-Thon, held from 9:30 a.m. to 1 p.m. Friday. First-grade teacher Shannon Rhodes at the campus's Edith Bowen Laboratory School organized visits from professors, athletes, scientists and other readers to show young students that reading matters. President Brad Mortensen said the event shows people of every age can take part, and reading areas will be set up around the Logan campus, including the Merrill-Cazier Library.
item.dc:creator: Todd Kunz, KSL

item.title: Former Utah Senate candidate sentenced for sexual abuse
item.description: Fourth District Judge Christine Johnson sentenced former Republican state Senate candidate Brandon Beckham, 51, to 364 days in jail Thursday for forcibly sexually abusing a woman in 2021, suspending a prison term of one to 15 years in favor of probation. An August jury convicted him on two counts and acquitted him on a third, after a 2025 mistrial and a hung jury earlier this year. The woman, who reported the assault months before Beckham launched his 2022 campaign, told the court the five-year ordeal had upended her life; prosecutor Alex Redmon sought prison, while defense attorney Jared Stubbs argued for probation. Johnson cited Beckham's lack of remorse, ordered him to register as a sex offender, and he was taken into custody in handcuffs.
item.dc:creator: Daniella Rivera, KSL

item.title: 1 adult, 3 children dead in Riverdale house fire
item.description: A father and three of his children, ages 5 to 12, died after their Riverdale home caught fire early Thursday, according to the Riverdale Fire Department. Crews dispatched at 1:46 a.m. to the house near 4600 S. 1150 West found it fully engulfed; the mother and three other children were hospitalized, one child in critical condition. Neighbors reported hearing a muffled boom around the time the fire started and remembered the family as kind and active in their Latter-day Saint congregation. Weber School District, where the mother teaches, sent grief counselors to four schools, and Fire Chief Matt Hennessy said a vigil is being organized at a nearby church meetinghouse.
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr and Mike Anderson, KSL

item.title: Mattel attracts takeover interest from Authentic Brands Group, source says
item.description: Authentic Brands Group has approached Mattel about a takeover that could value the Barbie maker at $6 billion or more, a person familiar with the matter told Reuters, after the Wall Street Journal first reported the interest. The offer under discussion is above $20 a share, and Mattel stock closed up about 18% at $15.04, though no formal sale process is underway. The approach comes a day after CEO Ynon Kreiz said he would leave for Paramount Skydance, with former Conde Nast chief Roger Lynch due to succeed him, a transition the Journal said could complicate any deal. Mattel shares are down 33% this year amid tariff costs, and an investor had urged the company in May to consider a sale.
item.dc:creator: Abigail Summerville, Reuters

item.title: Former daycare workers at Hill Air Force Base charged with 'roughly handling,' assaulting children
item.description: Federal prosecutors in Utah have charged three former workers at Hill Air Force Base's Child Development Center with misdemeanor simple assault of children under 16, saying much of the alleged abuse was recorded on daycare video. Karlie Brook Rainey, 29, is accused of covering a girl's mouth and face, pulling her hair and holding her in a punishing time-out in December 2022. Patricia Michelle Davis, 28, faces 11 counts for allegedly shoving toddlers hard enough to lift one off the ground in early 2023, while Allison Shea Ferdon, 32, is accused of yanking children, spraying one in the face and pretending to throw a child in the trash. U.S. Attorney Melissa Holyoak called the conduct disturbing; the base's Office of Special Investigations is handling the case.
item.dc:creator: Cassidy Wixom, KSL

item.title: Nucleus Institute breaks ground on Utah headquarters, innovation campus at The Point
item.description: Construction began Wednesday on Convergence Point, a campus at The Point that will become the permanent headquarters of Utah's Nucleus Institute when it opens in 2029. Created by HB530 and launched in August 2025 as a successor to the Utah Innovation Lab, the institute aims to connect universities, businesses and government to turn research into companies and solutions. Plans call for impact labs focused on problems like housing affordability, water and air quality, plus entrepreneurship hubs, event space and student housing. Gov. Spencer Cox, Nucleus COO Angela Smith and Southern Utah University President Mindy Benson spoke at the groundbreaking.
item.dc:creator: Logan Stefanich, KSL

item.title: Salt Lake business owner pleads guilty to laundering $17M in drug operation
item.description: Georgina Espinoza-Grajeda, 43, of Eagle Mountain, pleaded guilty Wednesday to conspiracy to launder money for using her South Salt Lake check-cashing and wire business, Multiservicios Lokos, to move more than $17 million in drug proceeds to suppliers in Honduras and Mexico. A 2023 Homeland Security Task Force raid on the storefront, which she shared with a snack bar, recovered 62,000 fentanyl pills, more than 30 pounds of heroin and cocaine, guns and large amounts of cash. Her employee Jesid Dadiana De Sutter pleaded guilty earlier this month and will be sentenced Nov. 23, and Espinoza-Grajeda's sentencing is set for Dec. 14. Of 26 people charged, 21 have already received prison terms of two to six years, and prosecutors say deals with the rest are close.
item.dc:creator: Cassidy Wixom, KSL

item.title: Trump launches midterm campaign push in Texas, Oklahoma as Republicans face tough races
item.description: President Donald Trump kicked off a 32-day midterm campaign tour with stops in Denton, Texas, and Durant, Oklahoma, as Republicans try to keep narrow majorities in Congress. In Texas he planned to promote truck tariffs at a Peterbilt plant and appear with Senate nominee Ken Paxton, who is in a tight race with Democrat James Talarico after a leaked recording of Paxton criticizing Trump's September convention. Trump acknowledged his administration had done a poor job of selling its economic record, while record diesel prices tied to the Iran war and voter frustration have made some safe GOP seats competitive. Alabama, Ohio and Nebraska are next on the schedule, Reuters reports.
item.dc:creator: Bo Erickson, Reuters

item.title: Utah senator proposes bills on data center transparency
item.description: Utah Sen. John Curtis and Delaware Democrat Lisa Blunt Rochester have introduced two bills aimed at giving communities better information about large data centers. The Data Center Community Empowerment Act would set up a Department of Energy program and toolkit to advise state, local and tribal governments on power, water, economic and tax impacts, while leaving approval decisions to local officials. The Data Center Transparency Act would require the EPA to report every quarter, and the Energy Information Administration at least twice a year, on data centers' water use, energy consumption, emissions and effect on household bills. Curtis pointed to public distrust of the industry, which has been fueled in Utah by the backlash over the Box Elder County project.
item.dc:creator: Bridger Beal-Cvetko, KSL

item.title: AI cybersecurity startup Armadin valued at over $2.5 billion after new funding round
item.description: Kevin Mandia, who sold his earlier company Mandiant to Google, has raised $255.5 million for his new startup Armadin, which deploys swarms of AI agents that probe customers' systems the way attackers would. The Series B, co-led by Andreessen Horowitz and Accel, values the company at more than $2.5 billion and lifts its total funding to $445 million. Reuters says the deal reflects a broader investor rush into defenses against AI-powered hacking, and Armadin plans to spend on research, training and expansion.
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: A Russian drone hits a Kyiv school as Moscow presses its aerial campaign against Ukraine
item.description: A Russian drone hit a Kyiv school Thursday without detonating while children and staff were sheltering, leaving a hole in the facade and no reported injuries, according to Mayor Vitalii Klitschko. The capital has faced near-constant drone and missile alerts in recent weeks, and residents describe exhaustion and anxiety; other strikes that day damaged a Dnipro River bridge and knocked the Parkovyi data center offline. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy ordered a review of partner deliveries of air-defense and F-16 munitions, as Patriot interceptors remain scarce because of the Iran war. Analysts say a large attack on Ukraine's power grid the previous day signals Moscow's push to cripple energy supplies before winter, the Associated Press reports.
item.dc:creator: Susie Blann and Barry Hatton, Associated Press

item.title: Peptides: Do you actually need them? A pharmacist's honest opinion on popular options
item.description: Pharmacist Phil Cowley, a KSL medical contributor, urges caution about the peptide craze that grew out of the success of GLP-1 weight-loss drugs such as Ozempic and Mounjaro. He says popular options like the BPC-157 and TB-500 "Wolverine" stack rest on almost no human research, while the GHK-Cu copper peptide has support mainly for topical use and growth-hormone fragments like CJC-1295 and ipamorelin have somewhat more testing. His bigger worry is supply: he cites a study finding 61% of roughly 2,600 peptides bought online were not what the label claimed. Cowley's advice is to wait for long-term data rather than gamble on unknown effects years down the road.
item.dc:creator: Lauren Tippetts, KSL

item.title: Heat-trapping gas once frozen in Arctic ground is slowly leaking and warming the planet
item.description: Thawing Arctic permafrost is releasing methane and carbon dioxide from long-frozen plant and animal remains, and scientists say the Arctic now emits more heat-trapping gas than it absorbs. Researchers including Northern Arizona University ecologist Ted Schuur and Woodwell Climate Research Center's Sue Natali estimate permafrost thaw could add roughly a quarter degree Celsius of warming by 2100, an amount often left out of United Nations projections. The thaw is also weakening the ground under roads, homes and pipelines, with more than 40,000 collapse features mapped across the Arctic, and may have contributed to a deadly glacier collapse in Nepal. The Associated Press reporting draws on fieldwork around Fairbanks, including an Army permafrost tunnel lined with ice-age bones.
item.dc:creator: Seth Borenstein, Associated Press

item.title: Woman rescued after 100-foot fall near Red Hollow in Iron County
item.description: Iron County officials are warning sunrise-seekers to be careful at Red Hollow after a 20-year-old hiker fell about 100 feet there early Thursday and hit her head. Spokeswoman Cassie Meredith said the spot east of Cedar City has become a favorite with students and that steep drop-offs are especially dangerous in the dark. Sheriff's deputies, search and rescue and a ropes team brought the woman out, and part of state Route 14 was shut down so a helicopter could land and fly her to a hospital.
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr, KSL

item.title: After 111 years, San Juan Record prints its final edition, but local journalism continues online
item.description: The San Juan Record in Monticello published its last printed edition Wednesday, ending 111 years of weekly print that had not missed an issue since 1915. Editor and publisher Bill Boyle said the costs of printing in Santa Fe, New Mexico, and trucking, mailing and delivering copies back to the county had become too much to sustain. The paper will now publish primarily at sjrnews.com, which drew more than half a million visitors in July, with daily updates, breaking-news alerts, an emailed weekly summary and help from its RedRock92 radio station. Boyle acknowledged the loss for longtime readers but said he is determined to keep southeastern Utah from becoming a news desert.
item.dc:creator: Alex Cabrero, KSL

item.title: Man arrested after allegedly shooting coworker following drunken argument
item.description: Beaver County deputies arrested 53-year-old Edmond Eddie Benally for investigation of murder after a coworker was found shot in the head inside a trailer at a Milford RV park. According to a booking affidavit, the two men had argued while drinking the night before, police had responded once, and a gunshot heard early in the morning was not reported. Deputies said they saw Benally trying to get rid of clothing that appeared bloody, noted injuries on his face, arm and chest, and found several guns in his trailer. Benally told investigators he was too drunk to remember and would neither admit nor deny the killing.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Community rallies around 8-year-old boy battling rare bone cancer
item.description: Sandy third-grader DJ Theorine, 8, was diagnosed with osteosarcoma, a rare bone cancer, on March 30 after a single X-ray of a lump on his leg revealed a tumor. Much of his time now goes to chemotherapy and surgery recovery, but he goes back to Beehive Science and Technology Academy whenever he is able. His mother, Megan Theorine, called the diagnosis a shock for a once-healthy, active child. The Bear Canyon Trail Run, directed by cancer survivor John Maack, is dedicating its Oct. 10 fundraiser to DJ's family.
item.dc:creator: Dan Rascon, KSL

item.title: 'Data Center Revolt' tour stops in Brigham City, stressing importance of public involvement
item.description: The Data Center Revolt bus tour, run by the conservative group Humans First, made its 29th stop Wednesday in Brigham City, where the Stratos Project Area proposal from Kevin O'Leary's O'Leary Digital has drawn heavy opposition. Senior adviser Kylie Kremer and Texas director Cathy Latham said they are not against AI or data centers but want local residents to have a real voice, greater transparency from officials and an end to tax breaks for wealthy developers. O'Leary Digital CEO Paul Palandjian responded that public sentiment matters, but said misinformation has led to threats against ranchers, landowners and commissioners. The tour was continuing to Cedar City, where Iron County approved one data center permit in June, and then to Flagstaff.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: Keith McMullin, former CEO of Deseret Management, dies at age 85
item.description: Keith B. McMullin, who led Deseret Management Corp. as CEO and president from 2012 to 2023 after years in the Presiding Bishopric of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, died Wednesday at 85. Former colleagues H. David Burton, Sheri Dew and Gary Porter remembered him as a kind, wise leader focused on people's needs. Before his 1995 call to the Presiding Bishopric, the St. George native spent 20 years in the church's Welfare Services Department and had worked as a Ford Motor Co. financial analyst. During his time at DMC, its media holdings including the Deseret News, KSL and Deseret Book went through a major transformation, and he received two Utah business awards in 2024. This Deseret News obituary by Amy Ortiz was republished on KSL.com.
item.dc:creator: Amy Ortiz, Deseret News

item.title: Senate unveils bipartisan deal tackling energy and data centers — but wind and solar questions remain
item.description: Utah Sen. Mike Lee joined Sens. Shelley Moore Capito, Martin Heinrich and Sheldon Whitehouse in releasing a 417-page bipartisan permitting reform framework meant to speed approvals for energy projects and lower costs. Among its provisions, the plan would make data center developers pay for the transmission upgrades their facilities require instead of passing that cost to utility ratepayers. Language on wind and solar projects stalled under the Trump administration remains unsettled and is still being negotiated with the White House. Sponsors hope for a Senate vote after the midterms, and Lee argued the deal should survive any post-election shift in power. The report is by Cami Mondeaux of the Deseret News.
item.dc:creator: Cami Mondeaux, Deseret News

item.title: Chinese hackers impersonated ex-US official to steal emails from AI experts
item.description: Cybersecurity firm Proofpoint says a hacking group it calls TA419 and links to China has been posing as AI policy experts, including former White House science office official Lynne Parker, to lure targets to password-stealing websites. The emails pitched AI collaborations to fewer than 10 people at think tanks, universities, defense contractors and law firms in the U.S. and Japan who work on AI regulation, export controls and national AI strategy. Reuters identified one recipient, former White House official Alex Engler, who said the invitation felt off and that he confirmed it was fake by checking with colleagues. Proofpoint believes the goal is intelligence on U.S. policymaking; the Chinese Embassy did not comment, and Beijing routinely denies such activity.
item.dc:creator: Raphael Satter and AJ Vicens, Reuters

item.title: Box Elder County data center plans quietly edging ahead though debate has died down
item.description: O'Leary Digital CEO Paul Palandjian says the Stratos Project Area data center in Box Elder County's Hansel Valley is in pre-development, not on hold, even as public debate has quieted and three lawsuits move through the courts. He said engineering, environmental and economic studies are underway with the Military Installation Development Authority, and a revised water rights application was due to the state this week. The first phase of on-site power generation would be capped at 1.5 gigawatts, and the company says full buildout would use under 900,000 gallons of water a day after recycling. Opponents are suing the county, MIDA and county commissioners, and two Utah groups have filed a defamation suit against Kevin O'Leary and Fox News.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: Pennsylvania tallies a fifth death related to measles as outbreak approaches a thousand cases
item.description: An unvaccinated Lancaster County resident has become the fifth measles-associated death in Pennsylvania, where 943 cases and at least 176 hospitalizations have been logged since April. Nearly every case involves someone who was not fully vaccinated, and roughly 40% are in Lancaster County. State and federal officials are also arguing over the count: the CDC dashboard lists only two U.S. measles deaths, and state health secretary Dr. Debra Bogen has threatened to withdraw a request for CDC field help unless the agency reports the deaths accurately, while HHS says no formal request has arrived. The U.S. has recorded nearly 3,700 cases in 2026, the most since 1991, and the local coroner warns the outbreak could worsen in fall and winter.
item.dc:creator: Deidre McPhillips, Meg Tirrell, CNN

item.title: US can deport the leader of Wisconsin's largest mosque on national security grounds, judge rules
item.description: Chicago Immigration Court Judge Jayme Salinardi ruled Wednesday that Salah Sarsour, president of the Islamic Society of Milwaukee and an outspoken advocate for Palestinian rights, can be removed from the U.S. on foreign policy and national security grounds. The judge rejected the government's separate claim that Sarsour lied on immigration forms. The case rests on convictions in Israel from 1988 and 1995 that Sarsour says came from coerced confessions; he has no U.S. criminal record in more than three decades in the country. Sarsour, who was detained in March and freed by a federal judge in June, plans to appeal, and his attorney Patrick Taurel objected that Jordan, where Sarsour has no ties, is listed as a possible destination.
item.dc:creator: Cybele Mayes-Osterman, Report For America, Associated Press

item.title: South Korea September exports rise 83.5% y/y to monthly record
item.description: Record semiconductor shipments, driven by global AI spending, pushed South Korea's September exports to an all-time monthly high, up 83.5% from a year earlier and well above the 62% gain economists expected, according to customs data released Thursday. It was the country's 16th straight month of export growth. Imports rose 26%, and the provisional trade surplus widened to $49.85 billion from $34.79 billion in August.
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: Utah-based counter-drone tech company secures $50M Lockheed Martin-led funding round
item.description: Fortem Technologies of Lindon announced Wednesday that it has closed a $50 million Series B round led by Lockheed Martin, which had invested $25 million in the counter-drone company in April. Fortem said the money will help it ramp up manufacturing in Lindon and expand deployments, citing growing demand that includes a Homeland Security contract to protect 2026 World Cup venues, U.S. Army work, and an August selection for a DHS counter-drone contract worth more than $1 billion. Lockheed executive Stephanie Hill said militaries need counter-drone systems that can be fielded quickly and at scale. Founder Adam Robertson has described AI-coordinated swarms of the company's net-firing DroneHunter aircraft taking on several threats at once.
item.dc:creator: Logan Stefanich, KSL

item.title: Box elder bugs showing up in large numbers across northern Utah, southeastern Idaho
item.description: Some homes in Cache Valley, Franklin, Clifton and the Bear Lake area are seeing heavy swarms of box elder bugs this fall, while other places have few, says Bryce Wood, owner of Cache Valley Extermination. Wood thinks a dry winter and late spring freezes left uneven insect populations; grasshoppers and wasps were also lighter this year. The bugs do not sting and are mainly a nuisance, gathering on warm siding and in nearby trees during the warmest part of the day. Wood recommends spraying them with dish soap and water, sealing cracks around windows and doors, and calling a professional if the problem continues.
item.dc:creator: Todd Kunz, KSL

item.title: Nearly 1,000 children were abused at three Massachusetts dioceses, state probe finds
item.description: Massachusetts Attorney General Andrea Joy Campbell released a report Wednesday finding that at least 275 clergy members were accused of abusing 944 children over several decades in the Catholic dioceses of Fall River, Springfield and Worcester. Most of the abuse happened before 2002, when the Boston Globe's reporting on the Boston archdiocese exposed the wider scandal, and Campbell said the dioceses often put the church's reputation ahead of children's safety. The probe, opened in 2019 by then-Attorney General Maura Healey, led to three referrals to district attorneys and charges in one Worcester case. Fall River Bishop Edgar da Cunha apologized to survivors, while the Springfield and Worcester dioceses said they would learn from the findings.
item.dc:creator: Nate Raymond, Reuters

item.title: Family of victim calls plea deal 'violation of justice' in Wasatch County child sex abuse case
item.description: Mitchell McKee, 61, a former civilian administrative director at the Wasatch County Sheriff's Office who was also a licensed marriage and family therapist, pleaded guilty Sept. 22 to a single third-degree felony of unlawful sexual activity with a minor. He had originally faced 10 charges, including child human trafficking and forcible sodomy, and the rest were dismissed under the deal. The case began with a January 2024 traffic stop in Heber City in which McKee allegedly admitted that a 15-year-old boy in his car was there for sex in exchange for a vape pen, and investigators later reported finding child sexual abuse material at his home. At the plea hearing, the victim's family asked the court to reject the agreement and send the case to trial.
item.dc:creator: Cassidy Wixom, KSL

item.title: Micron's AI-fueled revenue forecast blows past estimates, backlog swells
item.description: Micron Technology on Wednesday forecast first-quarter revenue of about $61.5 billion and adjusted earnings of $38.15 per share, both well above analyst estimates of $57.02 billion and $35.40, as demand for AI memory chips continues to outpace supply. CEO Sanjay Mehrotra said customer commitments under long-term supply agreements rose to $32 billion from $22 billion in June, and CFO Mark Murphy put remaining performance obligations at about $150 billion. President Manish Bhatia called memory the main bottleneck in AI and said new factories in Japan and the U.S. will begin producing wafers in mid-2027. The Boise-based company, whose stock has more than tripled this year, expects tighter supply in fiscal 2027 and 2028 and plans to raise capital spending.
item.dc:creator: Anhata Rooprai and Max A. Cherney, Reuters

item.title: Nuclear-powered AI data center proposed on state and federal land in central eastern Utah
item.description: Valar Atomics is seeking land near Price for an industrial campus that could include gas-cooled nuclear reactors, an AI data center and manufacturing on about 9,000 acres of federal land, the Bureau of Land Management confirmed to KSL. The Utah Trust Lands Administration board unanimously approved leasing more than 640 acres of state trust land in Carbon County to the company on Sept. 17, and board members mentioned data centers as a likely use. NPR reported that Valar's "Project Beehive" plans describe 456 small reactors, fuel production, waste storage and 9.6 gigawatts of output, while the BLM said any lease would first go through environmental review and public comment. Lexi Tuddenham of HEAL Utah questioned the safety planning and whether Utahns would get enough in return for taking on nuclear risk.
item.dc:creator: Brenna Donnelly, KSL

item.title: In the kitchen, Gabby finds joy after years in foster care
item.description: Gabby, a 16-year-old high school junior, has lived in five foster homes and seen several pending adoptions fall through, though she says the home she has been in for nearly a year finally feels comfortable. She learned to cook young, when she and an older brother often had to feed their younger siblings, and burritos remain a go-to dish. A recent visit to a culinary school, where she made pizza from scratch with a chef, gave her a chance to sharpen those skills. Gabby told KSL that changing schools has been harder emotionally than academically, and that she hopes for a family who can share some of the load she has carried on her own, ideally one with cats.
item.dc:creator: Ashley Moser, KSL

item.title: What to know about the terrifying FlyDubai flight bound for Israel
item.description: On Wednesday, FlyDubai flight FZ1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv, carrying about 170 passengers, fell from 33,000 to 17,000 feet in about a minute after one pilot stabbed the other and tried to crash the plane, according to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Netanyahu said the wounded pilot opened the cockpit door so a passenger and crew member could subdue the attacker, and other crew then landed the jet in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, after Israel scrambled fighter jets. Both pilots were hospitalized, Saudi authorities reportedly arrested one, and the motive is unknown. Coming days before the Oct. 7 anniversary, the AP reports, the incident has renewed questions about the threat posed by pilots themselves.
item.dc:creator: Menelaos Hadjicostis, Associated Press

item.title: Young boy recovering after being hit by car in Vineyard
item.description: The Utah County Sheriff's Office said Wednesday that a boy struck by a car Tuesday evening on Vineyard's Center Street is recovering and could be released from the hospital within about a day. He had initially been taken to Primary Children's Hospital in critical condition, Mayor Zack Stratton said on Facebook, asking residents to pray for the family. Officials have not released the boy's age, the driver's status or what led to the crash.
item.dc:creator: Devin Oldroyd, KSL

item.title: Senate blocks measure demanding report on rights violations in West Bank
item.description: A resolution from Maryland Democrat Chris Van Hollen that would have required the State Department to report on the killings of U.S. citizens by Israeli settlers or security forces in the West Bank, and on human rights there, failed 47-51 in the Senate. Republicans voted against it except for Rand Paul, and Democrats backed it except for John Fetterman. The measure would not have cut aid outright, but missing the report could have triggered restrictions; Van Hollen cited nine American deaths since 2022, while Montana Republican Steve Daines urged colleagues to stand with Israel amid the war with Iran. Reuters notes the vote comes weeks before the Nov. 3 midterms and an Oct. 27 Israeli election that could reshape policy.
item.dc:creator: Patricia Zengerle, Reuters

item.title: Utah 4-H communities rally around children facing serious illnesses
item.description: At the Weber County Junior Livestock Auction, buyers pooled bids to pay more than $41,000 for a goat named Santa, raised by 9-year-old Brandon "Chomp" Barela, who was hospitalized with heart failure a week before what would have been his first county fair. His best friend and fellow 4-H member, Tyttan Sappington, showed the goat for him so it could qualify for the auction, and the buyers then returned Santa to Chomp's family. Weber County 4-H coordinator Sharon Bee said the room went quiet when the goat entered the ring, and buyers began offering to split bids. A Salt Lake County auction this year raised about $15,000 for another young exhibitor fighting a rare cancer.
item.dc:creator: Eric Cabrera, KSL

item.title: Plínio Trump, Mick Jagger and Samurai Taxi Driver keep Brazil's tradition of joke candidates alive
item.description: A few hundred of the more than 7,800 congressional candidates in Brazil's Oct. 4 election are protest or novelty candidates, part of a tradition nearly 80 years old. They include helicopter pilot Plínio Vicentin Júnior, 59, who campaigns in Minas Gerais as a Donald Trump look-alike; "Henrique Barack Obama," a 57-year-old running for the Senate in the Federal District; and a 66-year-old carpenter from Goiás who runs as Mick Jagger. The AP explains the irony behind them: under Brazil's proportional system, votes for these candidates add to their party's totals, which can bring in more seats and public money for the establishment that protest voters want to reject. Joke candidates must still join a party and meet the same clean-record rules as everyone else.
item.dc:creator: Mauricio Savarese and Diarlei Rodrigues, Associated Press

item.title: 'Major' rockfall closes section of Zion National Park
item.description: Part of state Route 9 inside Zion National Park is closed indefinitely after a large rockfall Wednesday afternoon, according to park officials and the Zion Canyon Visitors Bureau. No injuries were reported. KSL said it will update the story as more details come in.
item.dc:creator: Devin Oldroyd, KSL

item.title: Audit sheds light on handling of complaint against Utah Supreme Court justice
item.description: A legislative audit released Wednesday found that Utah's Judicial Conduct Commission mostly followed its rules in handling a complaint against former Supreme Court Justice Diana Hagen, who resigned in May amid allegations of an improper relationship with an attorney who argued before the court. The auditors still said the commission's processes have weaknesses that could undermine its consistency and transparency. The report flagged an unnamed commissioner who questioned the complainant's credibility before recusing; KSL had reported that chairwoman Cheylynn Hayman, a close friend of Hagen, recused after raising doubts about Hagen's ex-husband, Tobin Hagen. The audit recommends clearer rules on how commissioners disclose conflicts and recuse themselves.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Woodruff and Bridger Beal-Cvetko, KSL

item.title: 3 charged with recruiting juveniles into gang
item.description: Salt Lake County prosecutors have filed their first charges under a state law passed last year that makes recruiting a minor into a gang a third-degree felony for adults. Abel Lara-Lopez, 19, of Kearns, and brothers Cesar Moises Santillan-Rodriguez, 18, and Victor Manuel Santillan-Rodriguez, 20, of Magna, each face 19 to 26 counts in 3rd District Court, including solicitation, drug distribution and weapons charges. A long-running sheriff's investigation found social media group chats in which adult members allegedly told juvenile recruits to fight rivals, steal cars, arrange gun sales and tag graffiti. District Attorney Sim Gill said gangs are targeting younger kids because the justice system treats juveniles more leniently.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Brazil's Nubank says it is not pursuing deal with Monzo
item.description: Shares of Nu Holdings rose nearly 7% in New York on Wednesday after the Brazilian digital bank said in a securities filing that it is not pursuing a deal with British digital lender Monzo. The stock had dropped earlier in the week on media reports of early acquisition talks. Nubank said its capital allocation approach has not changed and that its priorities remain Brazil, Mexico, Colombia and growth in the U.S. through Nu Global.
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: Man accused of abusing missionaries on TRAX train
item.description: Prosecutors want Paula Moala, 33, of West Valley City, held without bail on two second-degree felony counts of forcible sexual abuse filed Wednesday in 3rd District Court. According to charging documents, two sister missionaries said that in July a man on a UTA TRAX train kept asking whether they had boyfriends, then exposed himself and jumped on top of them. Detectives say surveillance video captured the incident.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Road Home community carnival raises funds to help Utahns experiencing homelessness
item.description: Wednesday evening's family carnival at the Utah State Fairgrounds' Promontory Hall raised money for The Road Home's shelter, housing assistance and support services. Tickets were $50, children 10 and under got in free, and the 6-9 p.m. event offered games, inflatables, food, a magician and other entertainers. Community relations coordinator Karissa Guthrie said about $100 keeps a family in shelter for a night and about $1,860 helps sustain a family in housing, so even small gifts matter.
item.dc:creator: Madi Vollmer, KSL

item.title: US removes Syria from arms export ban; Trump administration draws closer to new government
item.description: Starting Thursday, the State Department will review Syrian requests to buy U.S. weapons case by case, after a Federal Register notice removed Syria from the arms-export denial list under the International Traffic in Arms Regulations. That leaves seven countries on the list: Belarus, China, Cuba, Iran, Myanmar, North Korea and Venezuela. The change continues the Trump administration's warming toward interim President Ahmad al-Sharaa's government, which followed last year's sanctions relief, Secretary of State Marco Rubio's August removal of Syria's state-sponsor-of-terrorism designation, and plans to reopen the U.S. Embassy in Damascus after 14 years. The AP notes that with U.S. forces leaving Iraq, Syria may play a larger role in keeping the Islamic State from regrouping.
item.dc:creator: Matthew Lee, Associated Press

item.title: 'My dream has come true': Rainn Wilson sings with the Tabernacle Choir
item.description: "The Office" actor Rainn Wilson sang with the Tabernacle Choir at Temple Square during a rehearsal last week and wrote on Instagram that his dream had come true. The choir said Wilson's visit was part of a documentary he is making about what God means today, and that he also met with Elder Peter M. Johnson, played the Tabernacle organ and attended Sunday's Music and the Spoken Word broadcast. Wilson has talked about the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints several times lately, including joking on a Soul Boom video that he would join if the choir let him in and praising the missionary reunions he watched at the Salt Lake airport. He was also in town as a guest at FanX Salt Lake Comic Convention.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: After national push to relax surrogacy laws, Mike Kennedy says power should rest with states
item.description: At a Sutherland Institute forum on Tuesday, Utah Rep. Mike Kennedy, a physician running for reelection in the 4th District, said decisions about IVF, surrogacy and vaccine schedules belong to the states rather than federal officials. The question has reached Congress partly through Grindr CEO George Arison, who has funded a lobbying push and co-wrote an op-ed with Colorado Democrat John Hickenlooper calling for tax deductions, broader insurance coverage and new parentage rules for IVF and surrogacy. The Deseret News reports that Republicans remain split, with Trump having called himself "the father of IVF" while some conservatives warn of ethical risks. Katy Faust of Them Before Us argues the debate puts adults' wishes ahead of children's interests.
item.dc:creator: Brigham Tomco, Deseret News

item.title: Man sentenced to life without parole for killing woman over stolen phone in Salt Lake City
item.description: Third District Judge Kristine Johnson on Tuesday sentenced Kidus Chane Yohannes, 39, to life without parole for the November 2018 aggravated murder of 20-year-old Candace Samples. Prosecutors said Yohannes confronted Samples behind a now-closed Salt Lake City Dollar Tree over a phone she had taken from him at a library, stabbed her more than 20 times, and also stabbed Jeffrey Plante, a bystander who tried to help. Yohannes was not charged until 2021, after blood on his shoes matched Samples' DNA, and a jury convicted him in August. At the hearing, Samples' family showed a video of her life, and District Attorney Sim Gill said the sentence offers some, though imperfect, justice.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: Drive-thru menus are changing. Here's what restaurants are adding, getting rid of
item.description: Fast-food chains are reworking their menus around smaller portions and protein-heavy options as more Americans take GLP-1 weight-loss drugs, according to KSL Health contributor Miki Eberhardt. Because the medications blunt appetite and cravings for heavy, fatty food, and because rapid weight loss can cost muscle, protein has become a selling point for restaurants trying to protect their bottom line. Eberhardt called the shift a reversal of the supersize era and said the move toward better nutrition benefits all diners. Her ordering tips include skipping extra bread unless you are an athlete, choosing a wrap over a burger-and-fries combo, trying protein-focused mini bowls, and replacing fries with a side salad.
item.dc:creator: Lauren Tippetts, KSL

item.title: 2 weekend crashes in Salt Lake City leave 2 people dead
item.description: Salt Lake City police Detective Michael Ruff said two separate Sunday crashes are still under investigation, including one where the driver has not yet been identified. That evening, around 6:55 p.m., a car drove through construction barricades at 3400 West and 900 South, hit an excavator and burned. Earlier, around 6:40 a.m., a two-vehicle collision on the 5600 West bridge over I-80 killed a minor riding as a passenger.
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr, KSL

item.title: Senate blocks bill to address data center costs
item.description: The Ratepayer Protection Act, which passed the House 417-3 on Sept. 16, stalled in the Senate on Wednesday when a 57-43 procedural vote fell short of the 60 votes needed; only four Democrats supported it. The bill would have required state utility regulators to consider whether data centers and other large power users should pay the added infrastructure costs of serving them. Republicans brought it up at the urging of Ohio Sen. Jon Husted, who trails Democrat Sherrod Brown, and see it as a campaign issue ahead of the Nov. 3 midterms. Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer called it a toothless messaging bill and pointed to the Democrats' GRID Savings Act, which would make large data centers pay the full cost of grid upgrades.
item.dc:creator: Richard Cowan and Nichola Groom, Reuters

item.title: Native Americans wear orange for National Day of Remembrance for Indian Boarding Schools
item.description: Native Americans across Utah wore orange Wednesday for the National Day of Remembrance for U.S. Indian Boarding Schools, which falls on the same day as Canada's National Day for Truth and Reconciliation. Nikki Borchardt Campbell, an Indian Peaks Band of Paiute council member who leads the National American Indian Court Judges Association, said boarding-school assimilation policies still cause intergenerational trauma. She described a grandmother who ran away from boarding school back to Cedar City and a great-grandmother who tattooed her children's hands so she could identify them if they were taken. The Indian Peaks Band recently acquired the Panguitch site of a former boarding school where children's remains were found, to help preserve that history.
item.dc:creator: Arianne Brown, KSL

item.title: Woman accused of stealing luggage at Salt Lake airport handed 13 months in prison
item.description: Leticia Marie Torres, 45, of Salt Lake City, was sentenced Monday in federal court to 13 months in prison, two years of probation and $36,599.54 in restitution, closing out prosecutions tied to a January 2022 string of baggage thefts at Salt Lake City International Airport. Torres had pleaded guilty to aiding and abetting baggage theft from interstate shipment and to misusing a victim's credit cards; other counts, including aggravated identity theft, were dropped. Her codefendant, Brianna Marie Taylor of Midvale, received the same prison term last year, and a separately charged West Valley City man, Charles Masters, got home detention and probation in 2024. Police and airport officials advise travelers to keep bags in sight and pack valuables in carry-ons.
item.dc:creator: Cassidy Wixom, KSL

item.title: The world's largest oat milk producer has joined an unusual climate journalism campaign
item.description: Swedish oat milk maker Oatly is printing messages from the "89 Percent Project" on its cartons, starting in Europe, with U.S. shelves expected by January, according to sustainability director Caroline Reid.
