item.title: Exclusive-Meta testing a 'human concierge' for its new personal AI agent, Muse
item.description: Internal company posts reviewed by Reuters show Meta has been piloting a “human concierge” arrangement in which contractors quietly take over some phone calls placed by its new AI assistant, Muse. Meta told employees about the test last week, shortly after publicly launching Muse's calling feature. Muse, which has led U.S. app download charts since debuting two weeks ago, is built to carry out tasks on a user's behalf such as sending email, shopping and booking travel, and the calling feature lets it phone U.S. businesses to book appointments, check stock or gather contractor quotes. According to the posts, some employees objected on privacy grounds, warning that routing calls through call-center contractors could expose sensitive user information unintentionally.
item.dc:creator: Katie Paul, Reuters

item.title: Italian police find $3.6 million in cash hidden in apartment's walls, floors and furniture
item.description: Italian anti-mafia officers recovered $3.6 million in cash concealed in the walls, floors and furniture of an apartment in Caivano, near Naples, during a dawn raid Monday that produced 34 arrests. The Naples Carabinieri told CNN the money was in bundles of 50-euro notes wrapped in cellophane and stacked beneath floor and wall tiles and inside hidden wardrobe drawers, and officers hauled it out in plastic mop buckets to an armored vehicle. Police also seized 11 Rolex watches along with weapons and drug-dealing paraphernalia. Anti-mafia prosecutor Nicola Gratteri, who led the months-long operation, said investigators wiretapped cellphones that relatives had smuggled to incarcerated mobsters. Gratteri told reporters that a single home yielded 3.2 million euros in cash plus the valuable watches.
item.dc:creator: Barbie Latza Nadeau, CNN

item.title: Category 5 Hurricane Polo is an 'extremely dangerous' storm off the coast of Mexico
item.description: Hurricane Polo strengthened into a Category 5 storm off Mexico's southwestern coast on Tuesday and was expected to intensify further, according to the National Hurricane Center in Miami. Forecasters described it as extremely dangerous with maximum sustained winds of 165 mph, centered about 205 miles south of Zihuatanejo and stationary over the Pacific at midday, and said an aircraft would be flown into the storm to gather data. Mexican authorities suspended classes in several coastal areas as the system brushed the shoreline. Forecasters warned of flash flooding and mudslides, with 3 to 6 inches of rain expected in Guerrero and Michoacán and lesser amounts along coastal Oaxaca, Colima and Jalisco. Guerrero and Oaxaca have been hit by several powerful hurricanes in recent years and some communities are still recovering.
item.dc:creator: Associated Press

item.title: Semitruck driver accused of driving on I-15 shoulder without valid license
item.description: Irune Alonso Heredia, 35, of Des Plaines, Illinois, was arrested Monday and charged Tuesday in 4th District Court after allegedly driving a semitruck erratically on I-15. Prosecutors filed reckless endangerment, a third-degree felony carrying a road rage enhancement, along with a class C misdemeanor for operating a commercial vehicle without a commercial driver's license. The Utah Highway Patrol said it received reports of a semi weaving across the road around 4:50 p.m., with at least three drivers calling in, and charging documents say the truck passed a vehicle on the right shoulder. A trooper stopped the semi near Nephi and noted the trailer was still resting on the white line. According to the arrest affidavit, the driver angrily questioned why she had been pulled over before the trooper could speak.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Utah firefighters begin prescribed burns as preventative measure
item.description: Crews have started prescribed burning in the Heber-Kamas Ranger District, concentrating on the Castle Peak area. Firefighters are also working in the Pitt and Page area, where smoke will likely be visible to nearby residents. Dispatchers asked the public not to call in reports of smoke from these planned operations. Crews burned roughly 1,300 slash piles over the weekend, each pile being a gathered stack of forest debris that firefighters ignite in a single controlled spot.
item.dc:creator: KSL

item.title: ShinyHunters hackers say they breached FBI
item.description: The extortion group ShinyHunters claims it breached the FBI and stole data on thousands of bureau employees. In a statement on its dark-web site and in an online chat with Reuters, the group said it targeted the FBI in retaliation for a May 2026 bureau announcement that described ShinyHunters' techniques and urged targets not to pay. The group provided what it said was a screenshot of a defaced FBI job site plus a sample of stolen data; Reuters could not verify the screenshot, though a notice on the FBI job site Tuesday said it and the Special Agent Applicant Portal were unavailable. Reuters partially corroborated some of the personnel information by checking names and addresses against credit bureau records and previously breached data held by dark-web intelligence firm District 4 Labs. The FBI did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
item.dc:creator: Raphael Satter and AJ Vicens, Reuters

item.title: Aircraft company identifies 2nd pilot killed in Yosemite helicopter firefighting crash
item.description: Contract operator Precision identified the second pilot killed in Sunday's firefighting helicopter crash in Yosemite National Park as Ryan Cutter, 46, a Utah pilot who lived in Park City. Cutter and pilot Greg King, both Precision employees, were the only people aboard the AS332 Super Puma when it went down near Ostrander Lake shortly before 2 p.m. while conducting water drops on a wildfire in the park. The lake lies about 9 miles south of El Capitan and roughly 7 miles northeast of Wawona. Precision said in a social media post accompanying photos of the two pilots that they brought honor to the mission and would not be forgotten. The FAA and the National Transportation Safety Board will investigate, and first responders held a procession honoring Cutter on Monday.
item.dc:creator: Rebecca Boone, Associated Press

item.title: New York airport operations resume after disruptions across Northeast due to technical problems
item.description: Flights resumed at New York City-area airports on Tuesday with lingering delays and cancellations after damaged communications lines at an FAA facility in Philadelphia were repaired. The primary line failed Monday and the backup fiber optic line was accidentally cut by railroad construction crews, leaving controllers without radar or communications for hours and nearly halting commercial traffic. More than 600 flights into and out of Newark Liberty International were canceled Monday, part of hundreds scrubbed across the Northeast as every major New York-area airport was affected. Flightaware.com showed roughly 40 delays and close to 60 cancellations at Newark early Tuesday. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said online that clearing the backlog would still take time.
item.dc:creator: Josh Funk, Associated Press

item.title: Public invited to official lighting of new outdoor art in Syracuse
item.description: Syracuse will hold a lighting ceremony this week for a newly installed bison sculpture called Colossus of Growing Prosperity. The piece was unveiled over the weekend at the roundabout near 1950 S. 3000 West. City officials said the design draws on Syracuse's ties to the Great Salt Lake and Antelope Island, with the bison meant to convey strength, energy and community growth. The public is invited to the ceremony Thursday, Sept. 24, at Fire Station 31 beginning at 8 p.m.
item.dc:creator: KSL

item.title: Banned White House outlets cover Trump at UN as court hearing looms
item.description: Reporters from CNN, MS NOW and Politico covered President Donald Trump's appearance at the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday using U.N.-issued credentials, days after he barred the three outlets from the White House grounds. Entering the U.N. building, Trump told reporters he was surprised CNN was there and said the network should not be, referencing a claim that it would stop covering him; CNN has not said any such thing. Trump announced the ban Friday on social media, writing that the outlets should not be able to report what he called fiction and lies about the president, and defended the move again Monday. The three organizations sued Trump and administration officials Monday, arguing the ban violates First Amendment protections for speech and the press. They are seeking a temporary restraining order in federal court in Washington, with a hearing set for Wednesday.
item.dc:creator: Helen Coster, Reuters

item.title: Lawsuits allege Ozempic, other GLP-1 medications may cause sudden vision loss
item.description: Lawsuits filed against the makers of GLP-1 drugs including Ozempic, Wegovy and Zepbound claim the medications may be connected to nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, a rare optic nerve disorder that causes abrupt vision loss. One woman who had been taking a GLP-1 for weight loss said she woke up one morning unable to see out of her right eye; she works as a nurse practitioner and said she can no longer read, affecting her ability to work. Hundreds of other Americans have also sued, arguing they were not adequately warned about the risk. The drugmakers reject the allegations and say there is no evidence their products caused the vision loss.
item.dc:creator: KSL

item.title: Agent Orange memorial in Sunset sought by Syracuse Vietnam War veteran largely complete
item.description: A monument honoring people harmed by Agent Orange is nearly finished at Sunset City Veterans Memorial Park, the result of a years-long push by Syracuse resident and Air Force veteran Larry Kerr. Workers set the last of the large black marble panels on Monday, including one inscribed with the line about being wounded by dioxin and honored by all. Kerr, who attributes his own cancers and heart disease to Agent Orange exposure during his Vietnam service, calls it the largest memorial of its kind in the country. A formal dedication is expected closer to Veterans Day on Nov. 11. Kerr is pressing to finish the remaining steps as he deals with new medical findings of his own.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: Major name in US politics coming to Utah
item.description: Former U.S. House Speaker Paul Ryan will give the keynote address at the 2027 Utah Economic Outlook and Public Policy Summit, set for Jan. 14 at the Grand America Hotel in Salt Lake City. The Utah Chamber and the University of Utah's Kem C. Gardner Policy Institute announced the booking. Ryan represented Wisconsin in Congress and led the House as speaker from October 2015 through January 2019, and he was Mitt Romney's running mate in the 2012 presidential race against Barack Obama. Organizers said his talk will center on free enterprise, economic policy and the business climate in Utah. The summit gathers business, policy and academic figures to discuss the state's economic outlook ahead of the legislative session.
item.dc:creator: KSL

item.title: Trump says Iran deal nearing, Tehran offers Hormuz reopening
item.description: President Donald Trump said Tuesday that Washington and Tehran were moving toward a settlement, while a senior Iranian official indicated Iran could reopen the Strait of Hormuz within days if the U.S. eased military pressure and lifted its blockade of Iranian ports. Trump spoke after meeting British Prime Minister Andy Burnham at the United Nations, saying Iran has been talking to the U.S. and the relationship is developing, but that Iran cannot be allowed a nuclear weapon. He offered no specifics, and no face-to-face meetings between the two governments are known to have occurred since July, when an interim agreement to end the war collapsed weeks after being signed. His remarks came hours after a combative General Assembly speech in which he repeated a threat to annihilate Iran absent a deal and called for its complete economic isolation.
item.dc:creator: Gram Slattery, Parisa Hafezi and Antoni Slodkowski, Reuters

item.title: Wall Street expects Meta's AI agent to shape into a new revenue engine
item.description: Analysts have grown bullish on Meta Platforms on expectations that its AI agent Muse will become a fresh revenue stream and change how the company monetizes AI. Muse launched Sept. 8 and can handle tasks such as sending email, booking travel and completing transactions, offered free in a basic tier with paid plans at $20 and $100 a month. Meta shares have climbed more than 20% since the launch, outpacing the other large-cap tech names and adding over $200 billion in market value to reach a seven-month high; the stock rose 0.5% Tuesday after an 11% jump the prior session. J.P. Morgan analysts wrote that Muse could become the most widely used consumer AI application since ChatGPT, pointing to product-market fit, Meta's distribution and a free tier that makes trial easy.
item.dc:creator: Shashwat Chauhan, Reuters

item.title: Corporate bond buyers get picky with flood of AI debt
item.description: The high-grade corporate credit market has bifurcated, with investors bidding eagerly for bonds from traditional financial and industrial issuers while treating AI-linked debt cautiously. Portfolio managers say the concern is not default risk at hyperscalers but the scale and unpredictability of borrowing needed for data centers, chips and AI infrastructure, which has them demanding larger concessions and revisiting concentration limits. Goldman Sachs data show hyperscaler gross issuance is projected to reach a record $420 billion next year, up 60% from 2026 estimates, against overall U.S. corporate issuance of $1.9 trillion through August, a 30% year-over-year rise per SIFMA. Colby Stilson, head of fixed income at Brown Advisory in London, said his firm is being very selective within hyperscaler debt.
item.dc:creator: Gertrude Chavez-Dreyfuss, Reuters

item.title: Missing man found in partially submerged minivan in Box Elder County
item.description: Lewis “Lou” Balzomo, 66, who was the subject of a Silver Alert after last being seen Thursday, was found dead Sunday inside a green Toyota Sienna partly submerged in a canal near Fielding. Box Elder County Chief Deputy Sheriff Cade Palmer announced the discovery in a Facebook post, crediting the sheriff's office, the county search and rescue team and a SCUBA team for the recovery. Investigators believe Balzomo missed a right-hand turn, drove through a field and went down a steep 70-foot embankment into the canal. Palmer offered condolences to Balzomo's family and thanked the people who shared the original alert and helped search. The crash remained under investigation Tuesday.
item.dc:creator: Kennedy Camarena, KSL

item.title: St. George's gas average pushes past $5 per gallon. Is the state next?
item.description: AAA's gas price index put the St. George metro area just above $5 for a gallon of regular on Tuesday, making it the first of Utah's five tracked metros to cross that line in the current run-up. Logan, Ogden, Provo-Orem and Salt Lake City averages sat between $4.92 and $4.94, with the statewide figure near $4.96. Several counties had already passed $5, topped by Piute County at $5.34 and including Beaver, Duchesne, Grand, San Juan, Summit and Washington, while neighboring Garfield County was lowest at $4.89. Premium averaged $5.48 and diesel $6.56, both state records per the index. Analysts attribute the climb largely to elevated crude oil prices.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Zelenskyy to meet Trump at UN in push for energy truce with Russia
item.description: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy was scheduled to meet President Donald Trump at the United Nations in New York on Tuesday to press for a truce covering energy infrastructure. Ukrainians worry Russia is preparing to strike heating and power facilities this winter after escalating aerial attacks by both sides that have damaged ports, warehouses, ships and energy sites and hampered Black Sea exports. Zelenskyy wrote on X on Monday that Ukraine's energy sector, critical infrastructure and food exports must stop being targets, and that matching de-escalation steps would follow. He had cited diplomatic momentum after a Sunday phone call with Trump, though Russia, which holds a missile advantage, has given no indication it wants to pause the air campaign. Trump, whose approval ratings have hit a record low amid high gas prices before November's midterms, has voiced concern about damage to Russian oil refineries.
item.dc:creator: Tom Balmforth, Reuters

item.title: Trump, Greenland, Denmark sign deal in bid to end Arctic standoff
item.description: President Donald Trump and the leaders of Greenland and Denmark signed an agreement Tuesday during the U.N. General Assembly allowing an expanded U.S. military presence on Greenland, potentially defusing a standoff over the mineral-rich Arctic island. The deal stops short of Trump's demand that the United States absorb Greenland as a territory to counter Russian and Chinese activity in the Arctic, an outcome Greenlandic leaders resisted. Text released after the signing permits the U.S. to build a “Golden Dome” ballistic missile defense system on the island, which sits on the shortest route between Europe and North America and hosts the northernmost U.S. military base. In his speech before the ceremony, Trump characterized the agreement as giving the U.S. permanent control over security and other needs there.
item.dc:creator: Gram Slattery and Jacob Gronholt-Pedersen, Reuters

item.title: 'You should be ashamed': Park City councilman walks out during meeting on park wall
item.description: A Park City councilman left Thursday's council meeting partway through after colleagues took a different direction than he wanted on a concrete wall at City Park. The dispute came up under the final agenda item, when the recreation department sought guidance on the design of a basketball court wall at The Mine, the rebuilt community center at 1400 Sullivan Road slated to open in December. The 8-foot wall separating the playground from the court was part of the approved plans, but residents have objected to its size and the way it blocks views now that it is standing. A city staff report acknowledged the wall reads as more imposing in person than in the renderings while defending the design as intentional, meant to give the court a defined edge.
item.dc:creator: Cassidy Wixom, KSL

item.title: AI infrastructure firm Accelevation targets up to $5.4 billion valuation in US IPO
item.description: Data center infrastructure company Accelevation said Tuesday it is seeking a valuation as high as $5.37 billion in its U.S. initial public offering. The Miamisburg, Ohio-based firm and some existing shareholders aim to raise up to $720 million by selling 30 million shares priced between $20 and $24. The autumn IPO window opened cautiously amid rising bond yields and the first U.S. interest-rate increase in three years, but a queue of prominent issuers suggests activity is picking up: Nvidia-backed AI cloud provider Nscale filed this month, smart-ring maker Oura began its roadshow this week, and Anthropic is preparing a possible large listing later this year. Kat Liu, a vice president at research firm IPOX, said investors will grow more selective as choices multiply, weighing where a company sits in the value chain and the quality of its backlog.
item.dc:creator: Pragyan Kalita, Reuters

item.title: Moab woman shot last week dies from injuries
item.description: Moab police said Tuesday that Anzhela “Angela” Pronina, 33, died Monday afternoon from gunshot wounds she suffered on Sept. 15. Police say Charles Anthony “Tony” Nelson, 30, shot her at her home on West Williams Way and then killed himself. Pronina had been flown by medical helicopter in extremely critical condition to a hospital that authorities did not name. Police said she was an organ donor and that once doctors concluded she would not survive, her organs were recovered for transplant; Chief Lex Bell called that her final gift and extended condolences to her family in Moab and in Ukraine. Investigators are still conducting interviews, including with relatives in Ukraine, and expect to release more details next week.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: New justice center could be in Davis County's future
item.description: Davis County commissioners received a Sept. 1 proposal to consolidate county attorney offices and a new courthouse into a single justice center. County court operations are currently split among aging courthouses in Farmington, Bountiful and Layton, and a county project document says all three have security shortcomings and none meets current standards for safety, accessibility or capacity. The document argues that running three buildings costs taxpayers more, scatters services and leaves those security gaps unaddressed. The proposed five-story, 179,296-square-foot building carries a $171.2 million price tag, of which Davis County would cover $29.2 million. The plan also contemplates a state contribution paid through an annual appropriation over 20 to 30 years, plus revenue from a new county sales tax.
item.dc:creator: Kennedy Camarena, KSL

item.title: Bipartisan bill aims to expand health protections for wildland firefighters
item.description: Following one of Utah's worst recent wildfire seasons, lawmakers from both parties in the House and Senate are backing the proposed Wildland Firefighter Health and Safety Act. Supporters say it would direct new resources toward the long-term health risks crews face as wildfires grow more frequent and intense. Timothy Ingalsbee, executive director of Firefighters United for Safety, Ethics and Ecology, noted that vehicle and aircraft accidents claimed lives this summer while many young firefighters carry illnesses and injuries they may not recognize until years later. His group has endorsed the bill, which would establish a task force and an advisory council staffed by wildland firefighters to shape policies reducing workplace injury and illness. Ingalsbee said the central aim is early detection.
item.dc:creator: Shelby Lofton, KSL

item.title: 2 men charged in car loan fraud scheme
item.description: Yonder Jesus Reyes-Zabala, 25, and Jose Miguel Espinoza Araujo, 23, were charged Monday in 3rd District Court with communications fraud, a second-degree felony, plus third-degree felony counts of forgery and possession of a forged writing. Herriman police were called to a credit union on Sept. 15 for a suspected fraud in progress and found the two men waiting in the lobby. Charging documents say Espinoza had applied that morning for a $41,000 title loan to buy a 2025 Ford Explorer. The pair allegedly tried to withdraw the full amount, getting $15,000 at the Herriman branch and $10,000 at Riverton before the Draper branch sent them back over an irregularity flagged on the account. Investigators have indicated the case may be linked to another recent arrest.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: 'We lost our house': A deadly standoff left homes riddled with bullets. Who pays for the damage?
item.description: In June 2025, Cache County deputies responding to a call at the Valley View Mobile Home Park in Hyrum came under gunfire from Jorge Andrade, who had just killed his wife, Holly Andrade, and who authorities say was wearing what appeared to be a homemade explosive vest. Body camera and doorbell recordings captured him firing sporadically through the neighborhood as responders called for backup, and Cache County Chief Deputy Mikelshan Bartschi described the scene as extremely high risk. Resident RaeAnn Bott can be heard on a 911 recording reporting continued shooting. Both Jorge and Holly Andrade were found dead hours later inside their home. The KSL report examines who bears the cost of repairing neighboring homes left riddled with bullets after the standoff.
item.dc:creator: Daniella Rivera, KSL

item.title: Palo Alto Networks unveils AI-powered cybersecurity service using Claude, GPT models
item.description: Palo Alto Networks said Tuesday it will launch a business cybersecurity service built on advanced AI models from Anthropic and OpenAI to surface vulnerabilities across corporate systems. The offering, called Unit 42 Continuous Frontier AI Defense, draws on cyber-focused models including Anthropic's Claude Mythos 5 and OpenAI's GPT-5.6-Cyber along with open-weight models. It is designed to continuously probe web applications, APIs and cloud infrastructure so customers can spot weaknesses and likely attack paths as their environments shift, and it also recommends fixes including code-level changes and virtual patching. The company said the service will be sold globally via annual subscriptions priced according to the mix of models used. Palo Alto framed the product as a response to attackers increasingly using AI to find and exploit gaps in corporate networks.
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: Colorado State apologizes after derogatory 'Mormon' chants during BYU football game
item.description: Colorado State University apologized after derogatory chants aimed at members of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints came from portions of its student section during Saturday's football game against BYU. In a statement issued during the game, the school said mocking anyone's faith has no place at CSU, apologized to BYU's players, fans and church members, and said the behavior conflicts with the university's values. The statement added that administrators are addressing the incident with students. Longtime BYU fan Daniel Jensen said the chanting started before kickoff and recurred throughout the night, and that it involved a large number of students rather than a few individuals.
item.dc:creator: Dan Rascon, KSL

item.title: Taylor Frankie Paul announces exit from 'The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives'
item.description: Taylor Frankie Paul said Monday that she is leaving “The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives” ahead of Season 6 filming, tying the decision to developments in her custody disputes. She is negotiating custody with former boyfriend Dakota Mortensen, with whom she has one son, and with ex-husband Tate Paul, with whom she shares a son and a daughter. In July she checked herself into a rehab facility after months of public fallout from a since-closed police investigation into an alleged domestic abuse incident involving Mortensen. In her social media statement she thanked the networks that supported her and gave her a chance to return, while saying she did not want to continue under the current circumstances and addressing her strained relationships with castmates.
item.dc:creator: Margaret Darby, Deseret News

item.title: 10 years later, man sentenced to prison for role in teen's shooting death over thrown egg
item.description: Third District Judge Elizabeth Hruby-Mills sentenced Martin Antonio Cruz, now 31, on Monday to one to 15 years in prison for manslaughter, a second-degree felony, with credit for the more than nine years he has already spent in jail. The case stems from the July 5, 2016, killing of 16-year-old Paris Gustin, who charging documents say was shot while inside a Honda after an egging; prosecutors alleged Cruz and Fortunato Nato Villagrana used an AK-47. Ashley Gustin, the teen's mother, spoke at the hearing alongside other relatives and said she had sensed that morning that her son was gone. She told the court she struggled to find words for what had been done to her and her son, saying the killing destroyed her as well. Gustin also said she saw no emotion or remorse from Cruz.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: Davis County students run for shelter during hail storm, tornado warning after early release
item.description: Davis School District students are still shaken after Friday's severe weather struck just after early dismissal. Elementary schools in the district release at 1:30 p.m. on Fridays, and a tornado warning for Davis County followed at 1:45 p.m., with rain, hail and wind arriving in the minutes beforehand. Many children were outside or walking home when hail described as the size of ping-pong or golf balls began falling. Hill Field Elementary Assistant Principal Jessica Miller said parents and students crowded into the hallway and that she comforted one boy crying hysterically who had been struck in the head by hail before anyone understood what had hit him. Miller said staff scrambled to get students to safety.
item.dc:creator: Heather Peterson, KSL
